name: Social Design & Design Thinking for Urban Change　51
teacher: ディマ　クリスティアン
summary_excerpt: ※Face-to-Face delivery Global environmental problems such as climate chang......
subtitle: Transition Design: Co-creating Liveable Futures
summary:
※Face-to-Face delivery
Global environmental problems such as climate change, rapid loss of biodiversity and resource depletion are accelerating and have gained prominence on political agendas worldwide, while man-made infrastructure systems and cities have grown more complex and ever more vulnerable. Not least the COVID19 pandemic, the war in Ukraine and recent disasters have revealed the vulnerability of a highly interdependent, globalised economy. Today’s pervasive, interrelated wicked problems differ significantly in scale and complexity from those of the past that could be addressed, for example, with incremental clean technologies and local policy responses. Today’s new socio-environmental problems require more substantive ‘transitions’ in the coming decades such as major changes in energy, transport, community, housing or agri-food systems to name a few.
These system changes are ‘socio-technical’ in nature because they not only entail the mere development and implementation of new technologies, but also changes in markets, mindsets, user practices, policy and cultural meanings. The emergent domain of Transition Design acknowledges the fact that we live in ‘transitional times’ with permanent change now increasingly seen as ‘the new normal’. Accordingly, transition design takes as its central premise the need for perpetual, socio-environmental and socio-technical transitions to more sustainable future system states and argues that design thinking has a key role to play in these transitions. Transition Design applies an understanding of the interconnectedness of social, economic, political & natural systems to address problems at all levels of spatio-temporal scale in ways that directly improve the quality of life and safeguard human-centred development. It advocates the re-conception of entire lifestyles, with the aim of making them more place-based, convivial & participatory and harmonising them with natural environment.
In this course we will first learn to see and appreciate the complexity of so-called wicked problems —problems that are difficult or impossible to solve because of their complex and interconnected nature. We will then think about a system of metrics that helps us assessing the appropriateness of transition design and social design interventions. In the second part of the course, we will explore the transition design framework as it was proposed by scholars of at The School of Design at Carnegie Mellon University. It is one of many useful frameworks that helps us understanding how positive socio-ecological change can be constructed. Lastly, the course will conclude with a discussion of concepts like cosmopolitan localism and inter-localisation that promise a positive way forward towards forming more empowered, resilient communities in an age of intensifying planetary crises.
This course is recommended for students who can imagine themselves as change makers in the future and provides them with a critical language, some initial tools and conceptual ideas to move in that direction.

summary:
Given the complexity of modernity, how should we understand China in the 21st century? Whether you are a native Chinese speaker or not, "Understanding China" has now become an independent study field and an topic of daily life. Through anthropological studies, the course will explore key themes such as village community and economic life/family and kinship/gender, emotion, and private life/religion and folk belief. Ethnographic works employing a range of anthropological methods will be used to illustrate how different social worlds within China are produced and experienced. It also attends to embodied and emotional dimensions of social life by examining everyday practices related to food, Chinese medicine, and rituals surrounding life and death. By grounding broader social questions in concrete practices, the course connects large-scale transformations with ordinary experiences.
Bringing together classic and contemporary anthropological studies, this course invites cross-cultural discussion and comparison, encouraging students to develop a nuanced and critical understanding of China as a complex, internally diverse, and continuously transforming society.
goal: To enhance students‘ fundamental understanding of 20th-century China from a kaleidoscope of perspectives and to plant the seeds of curiosity and nurture potential research interests and goals about the complicated realm of China;

While the Han constitute the majority population in China, the country has long been shaped by the presence of fifty-five officially recognized ethnic minority groups, each with distinct languages, religious practices, and cultural traditions. Rather than treating ethnic diversity as a static mosaic, this unit examines how China’s multiethnic composition has been historically produced, governed, and reimagined, and how it continues to shape social and cultural life today.
This unit also explores religious life and folk beliefs as integral dimensions of Chinese civilization. From institutionalized religions to local ritual practices and everyday forms of belief, we will ask how spiritual life is embedded in social relations, landscapes, and historical memory. Through ethnographic readings and case studies, this unit invites students to reconsider China not as a culturally homogeneous civilization, but as a historically layered and internally diverse social world, where multiple traditions coexist, interact, and leave enduring traces.

summary_excerpt: ※Face-to-Face delivery Cities are rarely built from scratch. When we aim a......
subtitle: Theories of Place Making and Urban Practice
summary:
※Face-to-Face delivery
Cities are rarely built from scratch. When we aim at creating more liveable, sustainable and resilient cities as response to climate change, resource depletion, more frequent natural disasters, terror, or increasing inequality and social tensions, this usually has to happen by reconfiguring existing cities. It is therefore essential to know more about the people, institutions, practices and ideas that sought to form cities so far.
This course begins from the recent developments in city making that have emerged with the aim of creating more convivial places through pluralistic, democratic practices. These are seen to have positive impacts on streets, neighbourhoods, communities, and cities. Such new participatory place making ideas are rapidly dispersing world-wide. In this course, we ask the question, what are the reasons that city making, urban planning, urban design, urban governance or place making have become more participatory? From here, we will look back in order to understand which other ideas and ideologies of place-making and planning have been influential before and why have they been replaced and altered by newer ideas? The course examines the historical, cultural, economic, political, environmental, and other influences that determine how places form and how planners sought to control their development. Sustainability is one of the most important objectives of place-making and urban planning today. Questions of sustainability are ultimately questions about scarce resources, how we use them, and how they are distributed. Sustainability also involves social and cultural considerations and equity questions. This means that there are often winners and losers, risks and rewards.
Throughout this course we will explore the dynamic and contingent nature of place making practices and theories from four perspectives:
a) the specific activities associated with planning, place-making, and urban governance,
b) the different, often competing perspectives of people who plan, control, manage, and make our cities;
c) the relationship between state agencies, place-makers & civil society, and
d) plans, policies and projects as historical artefacts.
The class examines how and why urban plans and places are created, shaped, and reshaped by market, state and civil society influences as well as technologies at a variety of spatial scales - ranging from the neighbourhood and community level to the whole city and the region. At the same time we discuss the different approaches and strategies that place-making and governance professionals have been using to accomplish specific goals and objectives and how this in turn is informed by specific institutional, historical and spatial contexts.
The course is thus designed to provide students with a broad survey of the history of place-making and urban governance practices, a large number of practical, everyday examples that illustrate central topics to students, as well as a review of the important issues in planning and place-making theory. It focuses on the historical development of place-making ideas, the various roles planners and place-makers play in practice and theory, and the complex ethical dilemmas they face. Emphasis is thus placed on making sense out of theory and practice of how cities are conceptualised, planned, managed, governed, lived-in, appropriated, or contested.
Every lecture begins with an outline of larger social, political, or philosophical theories (e.g. system theory, marxism, neoliberalism, pragmatism, post-structuralism, post-modernism, post-colonialism etc.) and then details their implications for the making of cities and its relevance for the everyday lifeworlds of urban residents.
We will not only explore how larger social and political theories informed the making of cities but we will also discuss how these concepts ultimately impacted the everyday lives and urban practices of the residents of cities.

summary:
This course introduces students to the basics of English academic writing. Students will begin by learning how to write a coherent paragraph and then apply the skill to writing a five-paragraph essay. They will learn how to create an effective thesis statement, topic sentences, introduction and conclusion, as well as how to organize supporting sentences logically. The course will also focus on other essential skills for academic writing, such as paraphrasing, summarizing and citation. Practice for the TOEFL writing component is also incorporated in the course.
*Students will be assigned to a class based on their answers to a questionnaire on writing experience together with the results of the English placement test which is taken before the start of their first semester at SILS.
goal: ・Students will learn skills to identify basic components of paragraphs and essays, and will become able to use them to write essays.

・Students will acquire grammar and expressions which are more sophisticated and appropriate for academic essays.

・Students will improve skills to edit their own writing through feedback from their instructor and peers.

summary:
In this course students will focus on developing advanced essay-writing skills from understanding essay prompts to making better decisions about sentence construction. Emphasis is placed on taking a position in an argumentative essay, researching, evaluating sources, developing cohesive body paragraphs, logically developing ideas throughout the essay, and writing effective introductions and conclusions. Students will also learn essential skills in citation, paraphrasing and summarizing, and how to integrate sources into their writing. The ability to write with increasingly greater grammatical complexity and with subtle changes in emphasis and nuance, and closely edit for form and content is also a focus of this course. Students will read academic articles to be further exposed to writing styles, vocabulary, and background knowledge.
*Students will be assigned to a class based on their answers to a questionnaire on writing experience together with the results of the English placement test which is taken before the start of their first semester at SILS.
goal:
・Students will understand advanced academic essay requirements, and will learn to take an appropriate position, and argue and support it in an argumentative essay.
・Students will practice skills for using information from outside sources (source evaluation, in-text citation and reference lists) so that they can support their arguments more clearly and logically in writing.
・Students will acquire grammar and expressions which are more sophisticated and appropriate for academic essays.
・Students will improve skills to edit their own writing through feedback from the instructor and peers.

summary:
In this course students will focus on developing advanced essay-writing skills from understanding essay prompts to making better decisions about sentence construction. Emphasis is placed on taking a position in an argumentative essay, researching, evaluating sources, developing cohesive body paragraphs, logically developing ideas throughout the essay, and writing effective introductions and conclusions. Students will also learn essential skills in citation, paraphrasing and summarizing, and how to integrate sources into their writing. The ability to write with increasingly greater grammatical complexity and with subtle changes in emphasis and nuance, and closely edit for form and content is also a focus of this course. Students will read academic articles to be further exposed to writing styles, vocabulary, and background knowledge.
*Students will be assigned to a class based on their answers to a questionnaire on writing experience together with the results of the English placement test which is taken before the start of their first semester at SILS.
goal:
・Students will understand advanced academic essay requirements, and will learn to take an appropriate position, and argue and support it in an argumentative essay.
・Students will practice skills for using information from outside sources (source evaluation, in-text citation and reference lists) so that they can support their arguments more clearly and logically in writing.
・Students will acquire grammar and expressions which are more sophisticated and appropriate for academic essays.
・Students will improve skills to edit their own writing through feedback from the instructor and peers.

summary:

Students will also learn essential skills in citation, paraphrasing and summarizing, and how to integrate sources into their writing. The ability to write with increasingly greater grammatical complexity and with subtle changes in emphasis and nuance, and closely edit for form and content is also a focus of this course. Students will read academic articles to be further exposed to writing styles, vocabulary, and background knowledge.
*Students will be assigned to a class based on their answers to a questionnaire on writing experience together with the results of the English placement test which is taken before the start of their first semester at SILS.
goal:

・Students will practice skills for using information from outside sources (source evaluation, in-text citation and reference lists) so that they can support their arguments more clearly and logically in writing.
・Students will acquire grammar and expressions which are more sophisticated and appropriate for academic essays.
・Students will improve skills to edit their own writing through feedback from the instructor and peers.

summary:
In this course students will focus on developing advanced essay-writing skills from understanding essay prompts to making better decisions about sentence construction. Emphasis is placed on taking a position in an argumentative essay, researching, evaluating sources, developing cohesive body paragraphs, logically developing ideas throughout the essay, and writing effective introductions and conclusions. Students will also learn essential skills in citation, paraphrasing and summarizing, and how to integrate sources into their writing. The ability to write with increasingly greater grammatical complexity and with subtle changes in emphasis and nuance, and closely edit for form and content is also a focus of this course. Students will read academic articles to be further exposed to writing styles, vocabulary, and background knowledge.
*Students will be assigned to a class based on their answers to a questionnaire on writing experience together with the results of the English placement test which is taken before the start of their first semester at SILS.
goal:
・Students will understand advanced academic essay requirements, and will learn to take an appropriate position, and argue and support it in an argumentative essay.
・Students will practice skills for using information from outside sources (source evaluation, in-text citation and reference lists) so that they can support their arguments more clearly and logically in writing.
・Students will acquire grammar and expressions which are more sophisticated and appropriate for academic essays.
・Students will improve skills to edit their own writing through feedback from the instructor and peers.

summary:
In this course students will focus on developing advanced essay-writing skills from understanding essay prompts to making better decisions about sentence construction. Emphasis is placed on taking a position in an argumentative essay, researching, evaluating sources, developing cohesive body paragraphs, logically developing ideas throughout the essay, and writing effective introductions and conclusions. Students will also learn essential skills in citation, paraphrasing and summarizing, and how to integrate sources into their writing. The ability to write with increasingly greater grammatical complexity and with subtle changes in emphasis and nuance, and closely edit for form and content is also a focus of this course. Students will read academic articles to be further exposed to writing styles, vocabulary, and background knowledge.
*Students will be assigned to a class based on their answers to a questionnaire on writing experience together with the results of the English placement test which is taken before the start of their first semester at SILS.
goal:
・Students will understand advanced academic essay requirements, and will learn to take an appropriate position, and argue and support it in an argumentative essay.
・Students will practice skills for using information from outside sources (source evaluation, in-text citation and reference lists) so that they can support their arguments more clearly and logically in writing.
・Students will acquire grammar and expressions which are more sophisticated and appropriate for academic essays.
・Students will improve skills to edit their own writing through feedback from the instructor and peers.

summary:
In this course students will focus on developing advanced essay-writing skills from understanding essay prompts to making better decisions about sentence construction. Emphasis is placed on taking a position in an argumentative essay, researching, evaluating sources, developing cohesive body paragraphs, logically developing ideas throughout the essay, and writing effective introductions and conclusions. Students will also learn essential skills in citation, paraphrasing and summarizing, and how to integrate sources into their writing. The ability to write with increasingly greater grammatical complexity and with subtle changes in emphasis and nuance, and closely edit for form and content is also a focus of this course. Students will read academic articles to be further exposed to writing styles, vocabulary, and background knowledge.
*Students will be assigned to a class based on their answers to a questionnaire on writing experience together with the results of the English placement test which is taken before the start of their first semester at SILS.
goal:
・Students will understand advanced academic essay requirements, and will learn to take an appropriate position, and argue and support it in an argumentative essay.
・Students will practice skills for using information from outside sources (source evaluation, in-text citation and reference lists) so that they can support their arguments more clearly and logically in writing.
・Students will acquire grammar and expressions which are more sophisticated and appropriate for academic essays.
・Students will improve skills to edit their own writing through feedback from the instructor and peers.

This is a one-semester twice-a-week course for beginners. The textbook used for this class is published in France (Inspire 1, see:
https://www.hachettefle.com/collections/inspire

It also contains online resources for students to use in class and outside of class.
Students are expected to be active in class and to use French as much as possible.
The teachers may teach in French, English or Japanese, depending on the needs of the students.
The textbook content covered in class is the same as the one in Intensive French classes, but with less time to learn and practice in class. Students interested in studying-abroad in a French-speaking country are encouraged to enroll in Intensive French classes or to enroll in other classes offered in the SILS French program in the same semester.

summary:
Mark Twain once wrote: "Never knew before what eternity was made for. It is to give some of us a chance to learn German."
Yet, this course provides the basics of German grammar needed to understand basic sentence structures and to practice elementary communicative skills in only 60 hours!
The course combines the benefits of face-to-face classes with a digital learning environment with elements of gamification which enables students to learn and practice at anytime at anyplace. Instead of a single final exam, student's progress is continuously evaluated in a fair and stress-free manner. Teachers in the German program are continuously monitoring students' performance, provide regular feedback and actively support students with regard to competences development.
The German program is a recipient of the Waseda e-Teaching award.

Students are therefore expected to attend on a regular basis, be prepared to participate fully in the activities and discussions in each class, and make use of online teaching materials and interactive exercises provided on the learning platform and on Waseda Moodle.

This course serves as a bridge where students’ native language(s) and culture(s) and the target (Spanish) language and culture meet. summary: This course is a continuation of Russian I and is designed to further develop students’ foundational knowledge of Russian as a foreign language. It focuses on strengthening grammatical competence, expanding active vocabulary, and enhancing communicative skills across a wider range of everyday situations. Particular emphasis is placed on improving speaking and listening abilities, while also consolidating reading and writing skills, in order to enable students to participate more confidently in routine social and academic interactions.
goal:
Course Objectives
By the end of the semester, students will:
• Consolidate and extend their knowledge of Russian grammar at the elementary level.
• Expand their active vocabulary to approximately 1,300 lexical units.
• Master a wider range of speech etiquette for everyday social interaction.
• Strengthen listening, speaking, reading, and writing skills in Russian for practical communication.
• Develop confidence in initiating and sustaining dialogues in common social and academic contexts.
• Gain familiarity with cultural aspects of Russian society relevant to everyday interaction.
Expected Learning Outcomes
Upon successful completion of the course, students will be able to:
• Reading: Read short, simple texts drawn from a variety of everyday and adapted sources.
• Listening: Comprehend key information in audio and video materials on familiar topics, including references to place, time, and cause.
• Speaking: Initiate and maintain dialogues in predictable situations (friends, family, studies, work, hometown, health, weather, leisure activities).
• Writing: Produce short texts such as personal letters, memos, and greeting cards with basic accuracy.
• Interpretation: Summarise and present the main content of short texts in oral or written form.
• Cross‑cultural competence: Understand and respond appropriately to basic socio‑cultural conventions in everyday communication.
study_outside:
This course is designed for beginners and integrates classroom learning activities with independent study. Classroom sessions make use of audio and video materials organised around scheduled themes and are supplemented by regular evaluations, including quizzes on vocabulary and grammar. Students are required to complete compulsory homework assignments and to engage in self‑study using the recommended textbook, distributed materials, and online resources. The primary language of instruction is English, with occasional explanations provided in Japanese. Russian will be progressively introduced as a medium of communication during class in order to enhance language immersion.
Preview and Review may take around 90-120 mins. Each.

This course will be taught in Spanish.
Spanish III is a third-semester Spanish language course designed for those who have taken Spanish Intensive I or Spanish II. Students will continue to acquire knowledge of grammar, vocabulary, and expressions through tasks focused on developing the ability to communicate in Spanish. This course is designed to enable students who have already taken two semesters of Spanish (Spanish I and II) to improve listening, speaking, reading and writing skills in Spanish, while increasing their awareness of the Spanish speaking world. This course not only continues to serve as a bridge where students’ native language(s) and culture(s) and the target (Spanish) language and culture meet, but also serves as a step to an intermediate level of the language.
goal: Through this third-semester course, students will not only continue to develop their Spanish language skills, but also acquire critical thinking skills by examining differences and similarities between two languages and cultures. The ultimate goal of Spanish Ⅲ is to acquire effective and intelligent communication, critical thinking, and the appreciation and understanding of the Spanish speaking world as well as an awareness of cultural diversity in general. In addition, this course prepares students to be ready to take an intermediate level (Spanish Ⅳ).

summary:
This is an opportunity for non-native Chinese speakers to apply the basic language skills you have acquired over the past 1 to 2 years.
Even if you are unsure about your basic academic ability, you can improve while taking the course.
You have a lot of work to do during class, so you are going to use your own computer all the time.
goal: (1) Reading contemporary articles in Chinese precisely.
study_outside: Prepare and review at least 100 minutes for a week outside of class.
schedule_plan:
Each 100-minuteclass time slot consists of the following 3 main parts.
Part 1“Reading”: 20 minutes or more. Students select articles that are available forfree and read them, checking for grammar.
Part 2 “Essay”:60 minutes or more. Ask 3 polemical questions and write answers ofapproximately 120 characters regarding the article in Part 1. Students willanswer about 30 to 40 questions throughout the semester.
Part 3“Preparation for various certification exams”: 20 minutes or less. The expectedlevel is 3rd to 2nd grade for the Chinese Language Proficiency Test (Chuken)and 4th to 5th grade for the Chinese Language Level Examination (HSK). Otherthan that, students' wishes will be respected to the extent possible, just asyou can also use materials you have chosen.
textbook: Printed material
grading_method: 50% for works, 50% for exams. The examinations consist of recitations and writing down self-created questions and answers, and can be taken on your preferred date with the instructor's consent, approximately three times.

Eligibility for Enrollment
Students whose first language is Chinese or who have a Chinese heritage language background are generally not eligible to enroll in Chinese language courses offered by this program. Students who believe that a course is appropriate for their language proficiency level may request permission from the course instructor prior to enrollment.
*Students who enroll without obtaining prior approval may be required to withdraw from the course and may not be eligible to receive course credit. The instructor reserves the right to determine a student’s eligibility for enrollment based on the student’s linguistic background and Chinese language proficiency.

https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1Jhu5FEKMl1eeVuuWfjO-z0Huf6Ca7X6B?usp=sharing
(2) If you have any questions regarding course enrollment, please contact the Chinese Course Coordinator, Professor Tien Shi CHEN, at
lara@waseda.jp
Students are expected to attend classes regularly and punctually.
The instructor’s explanations are mostly in Japanese.

summary:

This course will be taught in Spanish. There is no prerequisite for this course. However, students are expected to have at least intermediate level of Spanish,
as readings, discussions, and assignments will be conducted in Spanish.
This course offers an overview of some of the most important Spanish-language texts that illustrate how Japan was portrayed in Spain and Latin America from the late nineteenth century through the first half of the twentieth century. Classes will focus on the analysis and critical interpretation of these texts within their broader cultural, political, and social contexts. We will explore how portrayals of Japan in the Spanish-speaking world took shape and evolved over time, and
identify the key figures involved in shaping these representations. We will study both well-known works by Spanish and Latin American authors, such as Vicente Blasco Ibáñez and José Juan Tablada, and lesser-known texts, particularly those by women travelers.
goal: The primary aim of this course is to provide the students with the analytical tools necessary to interpret key texts written in Spanish that convey diverse representations of Japan from the late nineteenth century to the 1950s,and to understand the cultural, political, and social factors that influenced their production. In addition, the course also aims to foster intercultural communication in Spanish through reading, discussion, and critical analysis, so that students can express their ideas clearly and confidently.
study_outside: Students are expected to prepare for each class by reading and reflecting on the texts posted on Moodle prior to the session. Any questions or comments, both linguistic and content-related, resulting from the reading and reflection will be discussed in the following class. In addition, before the presentation session, students are expected to prepare their presentations in accordance with the teacher’s instructions. Before the final examination, students should take sufficient time to revise the exam content specified by the teacher. Preview and Review may take around 90-120 min. each.

summary_excerpt: Linguistics is a scientific study of human language. People depend on lang......
subtitle: The science of language
summary:
Linguistics is a scientific study of human language. People depend on language so heavily in their everyday lives that most of them would find life without it unimaginable. And yet, they don’t really know how language works or, for that matter, how they acquired their mother tongue in the first place. Indeed, first language acquisition poses an intriguing puzzle. Every normal child easily accomplishes it within a few years without any special training (so the task must be very simple), but even linguists with many years of training can't duplicate this "simple" feat. There are many mysteries like this about human language, which is why the field of linguistics is fascinating and linguistic research has been very active.
Against this backdrop, this course will explain the workings of human language by introducing important theoretical concepts from modern linguistics. More specifically, it will introduce core subfields of linguistics, i.e., phonetics/phonology, morphology/syntax, and semantics/pragmatics. It will thus provide a solid foundation for intermediate-level linguistics courses (and beyond), which will equip students with necessary tools for investigating language and language-related matters. The course will also serve as a good preparation for any discipline that applies knowledge of linguistics.
CO202 (Introduction to Applications of Linguistics) a companion course that deals with applied linguistics, sociolinguistics and historical linguistics, is offered in the spring semester. Students who are interested in linguistics are strongly encouraged to take this course as well.

summary_excerpt: This course focuses on words in Japanese and English -- how these words ar......
subtitle: English and Japanese in Contrast
summary:
This course focuses on words in Japanese and English -- how these words are made, where new words come from, how the meanings and sounds of words change over time, and how individual words fit into the overall system of a language. That is, this course will introduce the basics of morphology-- the way words are built from parts such as roots and affixes. It will also consider some of the other interesting aspects of words, including etymology (the history of words), patterns of semantic change, phonological aspects of words (such as stress in English and pitch accent and rendaku in Japanese), and recent trends in word creation, including as the rise of blends, acronyms and use of characters in electronic communication.

summary_excerpt: [Course Delivery Method] : Face-to-Face This course focuses on matters tha......
subtitle: Genuine linguistics: scientific study of language structure
summary:
[Course Delivery Method] : Face-to-Face
This course focuses on matters that are truly linguistic. After separating linguistic problems from those that should be studied in other fields like sociology, anthropology, psychology, culture, pedagogy, history, religion, etc., the course introduces students to genuinely scientific study of human language. By the time students successfully complete the course, they will have developed an attitude of a scientist, rather than that of a prescriptive grammarian.
More specifically, using Radford’s textbook (Radford 2009), the course provides a concise and clear introduction to current work in syntactic theory, drawing on the key concepts of Chomsky’s Minimalist Program. By looking at data mainly from English, it will also introduce students to quite a few linguistic mysteries found not only in present-day English but also in languages like Japanese, Chinese, Korean, Belfast English, Elizabethan English, etc. Analytical skills gained in this course will be a solid foundation for conducting research in the following linguistics-related fields: child language, language acquisition, computational linguistics, machine translation, sign language, pidgin and creole, comparative linguistics, historical linguistics, language and thought, speech therapy, textbook writing, etc.
In more practical terms, this course critically reviews and revises school English grammar (i.e., prescriptive grammar), and in so doing, it will equip students with skills necessary to tackle real linguistic issues, including those related to English language education (which has been a big problem in countries like Japan).

summary_excerpt: Put crudely, pragmatics is the study of meaning of linguistic expressions ......
summary:
Put crudely, pragmatics is the study of meaning of linguistic expressions in context (linguistic and otherwise). Speakers of any language need to grasp different kinds of meaning other than the so-called “literal” one (i.e. propositional meaning) in order to express what they wish to convey. This is necessary also in order to clearly understand what other people have said or written. Most of the time, people perform this task without much effort, but explicating how it is done is no simple task. This course explores how meaning interacts with structure.
Issues to be discussed include meanings of the predicate (including thematic roles), functions of nominal expressions (including deixis), politeness, and viewpoint. The special focus will be on expressive meanings. Some of these issues are universally found whilst others are salient only in certain languages.
If the majority of students have not taken a pragmatics course, the first few classes will be spent discussing basic concepts in syntax and morphology so that they can later explore multifaceted aspects of "meaning" and also to apply them for analyses of actual language use.

summary: This course will examine the key principles of phonetic and phonological theory. It will begin with a review of classical taxonomic phonology, before moving on to modern phonological theories. Students will also practise producing the speech sounds of languages spoken around the world based on the International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA). Although examples will mainly be presented from English and Japanese to help students understand the theories, examples from various other languages will also be used to further explain the theoretical concepts. Students are expected to have a basic knowledge of phonetics and phonology.
goal: On this course, students will learn about current phonetic and phonological theories to help them understand relevant academic papers. They will also learn how to analyse real-world language data and interpret the results using these theories.
study_outside: Every week, read specified sections of reference books before coming to the class, and after the class you will be asked to do homework exercises which will be provided in the class, or read the referential materials. Preparation and review are expected to take 3 hours.
schedule_plan:
1:
Introduction and Review of articulatory phonetics
Discuss differences between phonetics and phonology. Revise IPA and articulatory organs.
2:
Phonation
How the focal folds differ in different phonations; voiced, voiceless, breathy voice, whisper, creaky voice, falsetto. How are different phonations used to differentiate words in some languages.
3:
Phonemes and Allophones: How to analyse speech sounds
Learn about the concept of phonemes and allophones, and how to establish phonemes in a language. Theoretical methods to establish phonemes: minimal pairs, parallel distribution, complementary distribution.
4:
Phonemes and Allophones: issues determining phonemes
Lean more about phonemes and allophones
：
how to establish phonemes, when there are more than one potential candidate for a phoneme among allophones: free variation, phonetic naturalness, marking convention, symmetrical system, natural class and pattern congruity. How prosody and phonation are used to establish phonemes as well as segmental differences.
5:
Phonological units (1): Syllables and morae
Learn about phonological units: syllables and morae: phonological definition of syllable and mora, and their internal structures: Onset, Rhyme, Nucleus, Coda. Syllabification rules: MOP, phonotactics, syllable weight and morphological structure.
6:
Phonological unites (2): Phonological words and above
What types of phonological units are recognized above the syllable? What is the importance of these units and how do they function in phonology? Consider their importance in phonological rules in various languages.
7:
Phonological rules and phonological units; Mid-semester test (tentative)
Relationship between phonology and syntax. How syntactic operation is blocked by the constraints of phonological units, heavy-NP shift rule in English. Reanalyse Japanese mora structure in relation to onsets of the syllable.
8:
Mora structure revised
Revised mora and syllable structures to consider the function of the onset consonants of a syllable and the weight of the syllable. Based on that, reconsider mora structure of Japanese words and how the onset consonant is linked directly to the syllable, not the mora.
9:
Features (1); Mid-semester test (tentative)
Understand phonological features and their functions in phonology. How to analyse speech sounds using features and the advantages for phonological analyses.
Mid-semester test on the contents of weeks 1-8 (tentative)
10:
Features (2)
Learn how to analyse phonological processes and rules using phonological features, looking at examples from different languages.
11:
Prosody: Speech rhythm, stress, accent, and intonation
Learnabout prosody, how speech rhythm and timing are manifested in languages and how to analyse these prosodic features.
Learn about intonation, and how intonation is realized phonetically andits linguistic functions in communication. Difference between phonologicalfeatures of intonation and their phonetic realization will also be studied.
12:
Phonological processes and rules
Learn phonological theories and how they are used to analyse various phonological processes and rules in various languages.
13:
Non-linear phonology
Understand non-linear phonology and how the idea of non-linear theory has been developed.
14:
Final Exam and Feedback
Final written examination on the contents of weeks 1-13. Overall revision of the course.

Important note: This advanced class will be held in German with English as an auxiliary language. Students are expected to participate in the discussion and read in German.
This course will give an overview of the role of language during National Socialism in Germany (1933 – 1945). We will analyze the propagandistic use of language during the Nazi Party’s rise to power, its use of language as a tool to submit the public and its function and perversion during the war and the justification of the holocaust. The class will also deal with the after-life of fascism in the German lexicon and the discourses on education and memory politics after 1945. Due to the current rise of fascist ideology, we will also look into new theories of fascisms and discuss ways to counter fascist ideology.

subtitle: Preparation for genuine linguistic research
summary:
[Course Delivery Method] : Face-to-Face
This three-semester-long seminar provides an approachable introduction to scientific research of human language. The history of language science is rather short, and there are still quite a few mysteries about human language, which any normal individual uses every day. In this seminar, students will be trained to be beginning linguists who can actually conduct decent research in this young but very systematic and exciting field.
In the first semester, students study linguistics as cognitive science, using Patterns in the Mind (Jackendoff 1994) as textbook. Questions that are asked in class include: “Do babies imitate their parents when they try to acquire language?” “Can we think without language?” “What happens to babies if they are raised by wild animals?” “What happens to one’s language if the right and left hemispheres of one’s brain are severed?” “What do language, vision, and music have in common?” “Can babies develop their own language?” “What is the language DNA?” “What happens when two people that don’t have a common language have to work together?”
In the second semester, students will read academic papers and critically review them. Then, they will engage in comparative studies of English and Japanese (or some other language, depending on students’interest). By the end of the semester, students will write and submit a term paper, which they can choose to develop further as graduation thesis in the third semester. Alternatively, students may also choose a different topic; in that case, they are expected to find another topic by the end of the summer break.
As for thesis topic, following the spirit of liberal arts, this seminar allows students to select virtually any topic of linguistic science; students may choose a topic from general linguistics, morphology, syntax, linguistics as cognitive science, English education, textbook writing, bilingualism, historical linguistics, comparative linguistics, language acquisition, etc. (as long as it is something that can be studied scientifically).
In the third semester, each student will work on his/her topic for graduation thesis individually. Students are expected to meet with the instructor frequently so that they can submit decent theses in time for graduation.
By actively participating in this seminar, students will be able to conduct quality linguistic research by thoroughly utilizing theoretical tools. If you wish to graduate with a sense of accomplishment, this seminar is for you.

In this seminar, students will explore ways in which linguistic theory and knowledge can be applied to actual situations; the main focus will be on second language learning and teaching, but we will also discuss other applications. such as in translation, lexicography, and advertising.
The seminar is conducted in English, but it is open to students interested in applications to ANY language. The theories and methods to be discussed in class are applicable to a wide range of teaching situations.
It is expected that students in this seminar will already have taken some classes in linguistics or applied linguistics. This seminar is not appropriate for students with no previous background in linguistics or applied linguistics.
In addition to work in class, students are strongly encouraged to do some volunteer work or paid work related to their interest, for example, as a volunteer assistant in language classes at Waseda or as a private tutor.

* University students’ English vocabulary learning strategies

* Attitudes toward the use of Taiwanese dialect in the media in Taiwan

* Metaphors and thought in Japanese and English
* Attempts to revive the Ainu language
* Translation of Japanese poetry into English
* Translation of English children’s literature into Japanese
* Translation of Korean literature into English
* Linguistic issues in the portrayal of characters in animated movies

summary_excerpt: F2F Digital humanities is a field that aims to produce new information by......
summary:
F2F
Digital humanities is a field that aims to produce new information by looking at humanities research through a computational lens, by preserving human culture through digital media and digitization, and studying how the digital affects humanity. Digital humanities is an interdisciplinary field at the intersection of humanities, arts, and social sciences on the one hand, and computing on the other. It allows scholars of more traditional fields to explore pertinent data from a new perspective and is especially useful where qualitative approaches, such as close reading, are not possible due to the amount of data.
In this course, the students will be introduced to the main concepts of digital humanities and gain an understanding of why and how digital humanities is practiced. The students will learn about current topics in digital humanities research and learn about simple tools, resources, and methods for digital humanities. Students will also learn critical thinking and method literacy in relation to computational methodologies. This course is a great stepping stone into more advanced courses on related topics. The final project topic depends on student interests and background and can be either a theoretical overview or a report of a digital humanities-related programming task.

summary_excerpt: In this course, we will look at the importance of games for learning forei......
summary:
In this course, we will look at the importance of games for learning foreign languages on different levels:
- We will discuss theoretical aspects of games and play and their use in education.
- We will test instructional games and evaluate their effects on language skills.
- We will design a game together that is intended to improve the skills of learners of German.
In the first part of the course, students are familiarized with central concepts of game theory and game design and learn about the significance of games in education. In the second part, we want to jointly develop an educational game on a linguistic phenomenon of the German language, which in its procedural rhetoric depicts relevant aspects of the subject matter. The students will work in groups on mechanics, rules, character design, sound effects, music and level design and thus contribute to the development of the game.
In the course of the semester, students will also be encouraged to review their own gaming biography, reflect on their methods of foreign language learning and critically question processes of the gamification of education in general.
In-depth computer knowledge or coding skills are not a prerequisite for participation. However, students should be willing to familiarize themselves with software and tools. Because the game we want to develop in the course of the semester will be designed to represent an aspect of the German language,
some knowledge of German and/or participation in the German language program at SILS are prerequisites for admission to the seminar.
Students of German I are also welcome.
The course will be conducted in English.

In this lesson we look at the use of games in education. We will learn about different ways of using games in the learning process and discuss the advantages and disadvantages of gamified and game based learning.

This interactive lecture-based course seeks to identify what it is people mean when they invoke the term ‘culture’. Throughout, we will critique the term “culture” in different contexts to examine whether it is a defensible position to justify the activities of different actors. To achieve this, we will need to examine our own position, critique it, then develop a defensible stance that defines and understands culture (and cultures). To do this we will consider how culture is transmitted, how it evolves, the different values it promotes, whether culture has boundaries, and critique the concepts of gender and nationality in culture. Particular focus will be placed upon five topics. (1) Identity, through which we consider how culture/s use tools to create and maintain individual and group identity. (2) Cultural Legitimacy, where the ideas of cultural relativism, consumerism (Pop v Mass) are addressed. (3) Language, through which we consider semiotic values and examine how cultures utilize the media to reinforce values. This will then lead us to (4) Taboo, wherein we will critique real world contemporary examples to consider our values, ethics and morality. And (5) we will reflect on the way our brains process and make sense of the information in the worlds we create.
goal: By the end of this course you should be able to recognize how the term culture is applied to sustain “values”. As this course blends practical components to demonstrate culture in context, you should be able to critique your own values and understand how you process information and identify with the world around you. You will be expected to demonstrate both theoretical and applied knowledge by the end of the course.

name: APM- Memory Culture and Memory Politics in Germany after 1945 51
teacher: シュタインハウアー　ハーゲン　フリチョフ
summary_excerpt: Important note: Intermediate knowledge of German is required for this clas......
summary:
Important note: Intermediate knowledge of German is required for this class as material and readings will be (partly) in German.
This seminar examines memory culture and memory politics in Germany after 1945, from early postwar narratives of rupture and responsibility to evolving public debates about remembrance. We study theoretical frameworks of collective and cultural memory, philosophical reflections on “Aufarbeitung,” and the interplay of state policy, civil society, law, education, and media. Topics include memorial practices, museums and commemorative sites, generational change, contested narratives, and the ethics of remembrance. Attention is given to politicization by contemporary actors, transnational influences, and postcolonial critiques. Students engage in critical reading, source analysis, and project work connecting historical interpretation with present day memory discourses.
goal: Students will learn about theories of memory, analyze policies, media discourse, and material form memorial sites. They will engage with political and ethical debates and do analyses, as well as train reflective argumentation skills.
study_outside: As a part of class preparation, you will be asked to read short excerpts of scientific papers both in English and in German, which will be posted on Waseda Moodle in advance. This preparation is expected to take 90 to 120 minutes.

summary:
Important note: Knowledge of German is required for this class. Participants should have a Level of A2 or higher (or have finished German 3 or Intensive German 2 at SILS).
In this class student will get an overview of German history of migration since 1945 and the according discourses, policies, conflicts and cultural as well as societal developments. We will discuss the political economy of labor migration (in the FRG as well as the former GDR), the different waves of anti-migration politics, the paradigms of “assimilation”,“integration”, and “post-migration society”, and discourses and imaginaries connected to the demography of the German population. The syllabus will consist of excerpts from literary texts, scholarly publications as well as newspaper articles and political speeches.
goal: Apart from an overview of German migration history, students will practice their reading comprehension in German across different text genres. The class will therefore not only deepen knowledge about German history and society but also teach important reading strategies.
study_outside: As this class is designed to teach reading comprehension and discussion using text-based knowledge, students will be expected to carefully read the required reading as a homework assignment. Students will also be expected to formulate questions based on the text, which will be used in class during the discussion of the topic at hand. Once during the semester, each student will be asked to open the discussion in class with a short oral presentation on the required reading.

Overview of the topics of the class and the requirements and working mode

Internal Migration during and after World War II: German Expellees (Heimatvertriebene) 1945
Historical overview of the migration movements within Germany following the defeat in World War II (and their historical revisionism)

History and socio-economic aspects of the so-called guest-workers in West-Germany
4:

The situation of so-called contract workers in the former GDR

Discourses and rising xenophobia towards guestworkers and their families following the declining economic growth in the 1970s
6:
“Wendezeit”: Internal migration after the fall of the GDR
Internal migration from East to West Germany after the end of the GDR and its societal and economic challenges
7:
“Asyldebatte”and Anti-Migration riots in the 1990s: The attacks of Lichtenhagen, Mölln and Solingen
Rising violence and hate against asylum seekers in both East- and West Germany in the early 1990s
8:
“Spätaussiedler” in the 1990s: Resettlers and late resettlers in Germany after the fall of the Soviet Union.
The social situation of so-called (late) resettlers from the former Soviet Union and their “integration” in Germany

A German Green Card? Skilled Labor Shortage in the Early 2000s
Controversies around the (economic) need of labor migration and nativist discourses favoring German workers

The 2010 “Sarrazin debate”: Normalization of far-right anti-migration claims
Discussion of the discursive disruption caused by (former) social democrat Thilo Sarrazin who claimed that Germany will fall apart due to immigration

The far-right protest movement Pegida and the concomitant establishment of the AfD as a new political force, both anti-migration movements

Overview of the polarized situation in Germany during the so-called refugee crisis of 2015 and 2016

Integration and disintegration as two sides of a controversial discourse focusing the situation of migrant and post-migrant people in Germany

Understanding the paradigm of postmigration society

summary_excerpt: Human lives have been embedded in art or technē—part of the etymological o......
summary:
Human lives have been embedded in art or
technē
—part of the etymological origin of “technology”—that makes the material world legible and workable for us, through which we create our culture. “Technology” and “culture,” however, are deceptively common terms. We participate in culture and are constantly surrounded by technology but seldom pause and reflect on them. What is culture? What is technology? How are the two related? What is our relationship with each or both? How do we live in a culture surrounded by technological objects, artifacts, structures, and institutions? How does technology change culture, and vice versa? The answers to these questions are complicated and open-ended. This course is designed to provide students with theoretical tools to begin asking questions for themselves and seeking better answers. Whether one applies these questions and answers to their job, life, or personal interests, the knowledge gained in this class facilitates the creation of a description of the world that is far more complicated and fascinating. Over the course of the semester, we will examine key themes in technology studies that involve the social, political, economic, and cultural contexts in which technological artifacts, services, and platforms are produced, distributed, networked, and used.
goal:
- Understand and explain a variety of academic positions that inform the study of technology and culture.
- Make connections between technological artifacts and larger patterns of sociocultural change.
- Apply the theoretical perspectives we have studied to specific objects (i.e., be able to relate theoretical arguments to specific examples).
- Be able to engage in a sophisticated and respectful class discussion of topics relevant to technology and culture.

summary:
What are Human Rights? What is the history of Human Rights discourse, and what is the place of Anthropology therein? Should Human Rights be universal or should they be listed or applied with reference to particular cultural worldviews? What critiques of the international human rights regime have been put forth by anthropologists thus far? In particular, how can international organizations that promote Human Rights, and state governments that sign on to international human rights legal instruments, benefit from the historical emphasis by the anthropological community on the notion of cultural relativism and respect for diversity? What is the role of NGOs in parallel to Anthropology in these processes? All these questions will be addressed in this course. The first section of the course will include revision of the history of International Human Rights Law. The second part will address the anthropological critique of that body of law and its applications. Reading intensive.
Generally this course will be conducted as in-class meetings and lectures, with possibly one ZOOM lecture, and one on-demand sections related to writing of midterm and final exams. We may have a guest speaker, details TBA.
goal: To learn about Anthropological method and theory, and about the history of International Human Rights Law. To learn to write critical anthropological essays about historical and legal phenomena. To learn and practice critical engagement with literature and ideas in Anthropology and legal studies.

summary: In this course, we will study the impact of social movements on the politics and culture of Germany. Social movements are defined as networks of organizations or groups of individuals that advocate for, resist, or aim for undoing political and cultural change. By analyzing the conditions under which social movements occurred in the German contemporary history and their repercussions since World War II, we will gain a deeper understanding of how Germany has developed into a liberal democracy.
goal:
At the end of this course, students will be able to:
• Define what a social movement is.
• Explain, with historical examples, when and why social movements occur, how they organize, what movements do, and who participates.
• Understand, how social change and social movements relate.
• Explain, how social movements like the student movement of the 1960s, the women's movement, the lesbian and gay movement, the environmental movement, the alter-globalization movement, but also the neo-Nazi contributed to political and cultural change in the history of Germany.

Half the content will be on-demand videos, and the other half (Thursday classes) will be mostly in-class with the possibility of some "F2F" classes taking place on Zoom.
In this course, students will expand on their programming skills from a digital humanities perspective. This course is a continuation of the Python Programming for Digital Humanities course from the previous semester, but the focus is on the application as much as intermediate programming skills. We will focus on Python pandas for data analysis and data manipulation and use matplotlib for visualization. We will also learn about version control using git. The latter half of the course focuses on social media analysis including network analysis, topic modeling, and sentiment analysis.
It is strongly recommended that students have taken the intermediate course “Python Programming for Digital Humanities” or a similar one before taking this course. A background in R/Java/C/Perl/Ruby and a willingness to learn Python would also cover these prerequisites. THIS COURSE REQUIRES BASIC PROGRAMMING SKILLS

summary: This semester will continue our discussion of Anthropology and Sociology of Law. Our focus this semester will be the Legal and Social Anthropology of Modern practices of Witchcraft, Sorcery and Magic.  Main questions to consider include:  How do modern discourses about Modernity, Science and Rationality oppose themselves to Witchcraft, Sorcery and Magic and to other seemingly 'imaginary' or 'irrational' practices? How, conversely, are Witchcraft, Sorcery,  and Magic opposed to, or how do they exist in parallel with, Scientific or Rational understandings of the physical and spiritual worlds?  How are Witchcraft, Sorcery and Magic used by people to act, sometimes with extreme violence, against other members of their societies, oftentimes women? How have modern legal systems legislated or handled cases of violence by Witchcraft or Sorcery?  How have Social Anthropologists apprehended Witchcraft and Magic differently than governing bodies and their legal systems, and how can anthropological and historical perspectives be used to promote understanding of articulations of modern witchcraft and magic practices in post-colonial contexts?

summary_excerpt: As with in the Spring Semester, this advanced seminar provides students th......
subtitle: One Long Conversation: Transoceanian Approaches to Culture, Gender, and Identity
summary:
As with in the Spring Semester, this advanced seminar provides students the chance to build upon their previous studies of cultural studies, gender studies, and postcolonial studies, particularly in the context of Pacific and Asian regional studies. However, this seminar also has a significant writing component to it, geared toward students in the final stages of completing their graduation theses, and this is why there is an additional period of class built into the schedule for final semester students only. Aside from this, like the spring semester, this zemi also engages with creative representation in film and contemporary art. It is especially an opportunity for mainly students who have already studied with this instructor to apply their knowledge to specialized individual studies around themes of interest in cultural studies. Adding to what has been discussed in previous courses and seminars with this instructor, this course allows students to work toward a senior thesis project in terms of the intersections between gender/identity/sexuality/culture/region/militarism/tourism/race, etc. to further their understanding of cultural studies, gender studies, and Pacific Studies, and to develop their own individualized projects that cater to their particular interests. Since this is a seminar for advanced students, much of the content will revolve around sharing lively discussion that is of mutual interest to all students, and working together on your independent graduation projects.
This seminar is offered in a group discussion-based format, focused primarily around individual student research projects, in which students learn from each other at different levels. All students do shared readings and explore different topics together each semester, and each semester the instructor curates a unique cultural studies/history/gender studies/ethnography theme that we all focus upon. In general, juniors (3rd year students) help to lead the readings about the main theme and work toward writing a general reflective essay on that theme at the end of the semester; whereas seniors (4th year students) present and teach the seminar about the research that they are doing on their respective topics, with the goal of writing chapters toward their senior thesis due at the end of the year. Together, we also will pursue group projects and different outreach activities, as well as possible extracurricular activities, based on the proposals of all participants in the seminar.
Each semester, the collective conversation theme is different, and we cycle through these themes as each cohort passes through the seminar. For example, in previous semesters we have considered "Vulnerable Histories;" "Reading with the Senses;" "Mythologies of the Everyday World," and other themes. In 2020-2021, due to the pandemic, we took on more projects related to global turmoil, vulnerability, trauma, and self-reflexivity as we transitioned to a temporary all online format. In future semesters, we will gradually transition back to in-person classes little by little when it is advisable to do so, but on Zoom we make creative use of breakout rooms to divide students into interesting cohorts based around their biggest interests, to maximize learning. At other points in our seminar, we spend time thinking about urban cultures and communities in Tokyo, sensory learning, contemporary art, indigenous communities in Oceania, queer studies and masculinities, and so on. In the 2020-2021 period, we aimed to welcome guest speakers who were successful contemporary artists in Japan to come and talk with us about the theme of "decolonizing Japan," which gave students unique opportunities to think about how to take action in their own lives and with their own talents. We will continue to pursue such activities in coming semesters as well. We may also connect Greg's students in the Graduate School of International Culture and Communication Studies as well as art students in other parts of Japan that Greg mentors, as a way of expanding our awareness and creativity. As always, incoming new students to the seminar will easily be able to access all of our archived previous readings and discussions and encouraged to learn from their sempai by reading their theses.
Students who have already studied with this instructor are strongly encouraged to join this seminar (especially those who have taken all of the instructor's courses, including first year seminars), while those who have not taken previous courses should first consider taking the instructor’s intermediate seminar and other lecture courses, since there is prerequisite knowledge that you should know in order to make the most of this seminar. This is meant to be a lively but rigorous seminar, but only with a limited number of participants, so that everyone can participate and contribute fully. Because of this, not everyone who applies for the seminar can be admitted, and in principle, some semesters allow more students than others, based on the number of students currently enrolled. Please keep this in mind if you apply.
goal: Throughout this semester, students will expand upon the nuanced understanding of the core themes discussed in previous courses they have taken with this instructor, in terms of how these relate to the Pacific and Asian region and their own interests. They will also cultivate and hone their abilities to do successful and interesting, stimulating, unique research and writing for their senior projects. You will be expected to utilize cultural studies and gender studies-inspired approaches to problems such as conflict, marginalized groups, vulnerable communities, militarism, globalization, and environment, through readings assigned in the first part of the seminar, and later through independent research toward your senior project. This thesis project will be crafted using unique and interesting methodologies which we will also discuss extensively in our seminar, by doing readings in ethnographic and cultural studies techniques, as well as self-reflexive writing, filmmaking, photography, and other creative approaches.
study_outside: Students will be expected to lead seminar sessions and to present on their work actively, as well as to have prepared for each session by doing the assigned readings. However, this seminar is meant to be a relaxed and friendly environment for the exchange of ideas, so students are encouraged to share whatever insights they have and express themselves creatively. Aside from assigned readings, students will write short essays and conduct their own independent research, all of which will contribute toward their senior thesis project, required for graduation.
schedule_plan: This is a two-credit seminar course which will meet once a week for one period; however, since advanced students should be working towards their senior theses as early as possible, we will aim to meet additionally (sometimes individually) and develop a rapport to discuss ideas in fruitful and meaningful ways. Based on the number of students and the backgrounds of each student, we will adjust our semester schedule. All students will be required to do all course readings and to make presentations in groups and individually, based on your individual projects. A detailed schedule will be produced in the first weeks of the semester, in consultation with all students.

reference: This course is part of a suite of courses at SILS in the area of gender and cultural studies in Asia and Oceania, which connects to the courses this instructor teaches about colonialism and globalization in the Pacific Islands. Please refer to the courses “Pacific Perspectives on Empire, War, and Globalization,” “The Pacific in the 21st Century World,” and “Contemporary Intersections of Gender, Identity, and Culture,” and seminar courses at other levels for examples of the approach we will use.
grading_method:
1) THESIS (separately graded for senior students): All students in this seminar are expected to complete a senior research project resulting in the form of either a full written thesis (word count/pages, etc. are to be discussed, although the minimum be basically the same as most seminars), or a “portfolio,” which is a combination of a detailed writing component (less than the length of a thesis) and another kind of media— such as a film, a work of art, a performance, etc. If you choose the latter option, especially, you must discuss this with me at least 6 months in advance of your submission to get approval.
2) ENGAGEMENT (30% of your grade): All students must come to the seminar on time, every week on time at 16:30, unless they have informed me in advance and have a compelling reason to be absent or late. See below.
3) ACTIVE DISCUSSION (40% of your grade): All students must be active and ready to speak, having done the readings or assigned tasks, and prepared to share their thoughts. However, it is wise to really DO THE READINGS before you start speaking about them. Sometimes students like to talk a lot just to distract from the fact that they haven’t actually prepared. Base your opinions on proper reading and research wherever possible.
4) SMALL TASKS/READINGS (30%): As noted above, you will have something to read and prepare each week, which will be posted to CourseN@vi. Sometimes I may also ask for a reflective assignment to help focus discussions the following week. Additionally, ALL important previous readings from this seminar, from previous semesters (because each semester is different) are archived on the CourseN@vi page for this class. Sometimes I will ask incoming students to review some of those materials to get a better idea of what conversations have been going on before they came. I strongly suggest that new students familiarize yourself with our ongoing conversation.

summary:
※Face-to-Face Delivery
This advanced seminar is intended for students who have a keen interest in cities, architecture, public spaces and urban life in general. Despite representing only about 2% of the geographic space, cities accommodate currently over 55% of the global population, produce 80% of greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, consume 75% of the world's energy and 80% of its resources. On the other hand urban areas also generate 93% of the world's patented inventions. City governments face a wide range of challenges: they need to produce prosperity and innovations but also well-being and sustainability. Cities are to be green and resilient but also culturally vibrant. On top of this, cities are integration machines that integrate growing populations from different ethnic, religious, cultural, and socio-economic backgrounds. To cope with these pressing issues, change makers are not only needed in ministries and city halls but also in the business world, in non-profits, independent consultancies, or in academia. This seminar, will provide you with a first step to become an urban change maker.
This 3-semester long advanced seminar offers students the opportunity to sharpen their understanding about urbanisation issues, urban governance, place-making, and the social production of space. In this course students develop an own, individualised urban studies or urbanism-related research project from an initial research proposal (1rst semester), over an annotated bibliography (2nd semester), a midterm paper (2nd semester), and conclude the course in the 3rd semester with a full graduation thesis.
Possible research subjects may be sustainability transitions, creative neighbourhoods and social innovators, new urban commons, community resilience, participatory place-making, social construction of space, contestations of public space, environmental and economic gentrification among other topics that help us to understand how socio-cultural, historical, economic and political aspects influence the emergence of cities and communities in an era that Neil Brenner and Christian Schmid have identified as "planetary urbanisation". In fact, students are encouraged to approach the subject 'city' from any disciplinary angle, be it social, cultural, historical, environmental, economic, or artistic.
Students are expected to begin the work on their graduation theses at an early stage in this seminar. They will present their own work on a regular basis, and participate actively in the discussion of the work presented by other members of the class. Class room sessions will be supplemented with different urban walks, during which students will learn about different urbanisation issues and different socio-spatial settings. The learning culture of the seminar is similar to that found at graduate school level, with all members, including the instructor, being active co-learners. This seminar will enable students to enter urbanism and urban planning related graduate programs and only highly dedicated students should consider applying.
For students who take this Zemi in the first (of three) semesters the focus will be on exploring different urban settings in Tokyo and familiarise themselves with urban studies research methods. Students will present the impressions of their urban walks as visual essays in class. At the end of the first semester a first draft proposal for their graduation research will be completed.
Students for whom this is the third semester of the Zemi will solely concentrate on the writing of their graduation thesis.
The first period will be reserved for the first semester Zemi students and the following period will be used for presentations and discussions of the graduation research projects of third semester students.

summary_excerpt: This seminar offers a critical look at data science, data analysis, and b......
subtitle: NLP and Digital Humanities
summary:
This seminar offers a critical look at data science, data analysis, and big data in particular. There is increasing concern over biased algorithms and how these affect fairness. The social impact of such algorithmic approaches is explored critically from an NLP and DH perspective.
Large datasets are becoming the norm in many fields, and people tend to accept that numbers do not lie. However, there are many ways how dehumanizing data can lead to a skewed or biased outcome. In this seminar, we will explore skewed data, bias in machine learning algorithms, and how to present data “ethically”. We discuss concepts such as actuarial fairness and algorithmic fairness. Basic programming skills are required.
In the fall semester we participate in a SemEval task learning hands-on NLP methods.
goal: After successful completion of this course, students will be able to explain the core ethical issues with big data and machine learning as well as understand how biases hide in data and what the implications for downstream applications are. Students will also understand why open science is important and be able to explain what digital research ethics are.

subtitle: Introduction to Financial Accounting
summary:
※Online(Live Stream) with On-Demand Recorded Video
Accounting is the process of identifying, recording, and reporting of economic activities. Accounting serves a vital role in our economy. It is a language to present the financial condition of a business, non-business or other entity as well as how an entity performed financially in a given time period. There are many people who rely on accounting information for their decision making, including investors, creditors, regulators as well as executives and managers who run businesses. In this course, you will learn a fundamental framework and concept for financial accounting, which is used by for-profit business enterprises mainly in their external reporting. In any business, financial accounting is imperative; it is simply impossible to understand a business without understanding accounting. The primary objectives of this course are for you to understand (1) the basic concept of financial accounting, (2) how it is processed, and (3) how it is used. There are no pre-requisites for this course, nor should you have accounting background or any specialized knowledge, as long as you understand basic arithmetic.
