study_outside: Students are expected to finish reading assignments before each class that will be announced in the class. Each of the reading assignments takes approximately 60 minutes. In addition, an assignment with quizzes and exercises will be given every week through the on-line platform. They will cover not only the topics covered by the reading assignments but also the topics presented and discussed in the class. It takes approximately 60 to 120 minutes to finish each assignment.

1:
Class No.1: Introduction to Accounting (1 of 2)
Accounting is defined. How does accounting work and how is it used? What are the building blocks behind accounting? Why does accounting matter to us?
2:
Class No.2: Introduction to Accounting (2 of 2)
In this class, the basic accounting equation is presented. This class also covers what financial statements are comprised of and some of the key points in reading financial statements.
3:
Class No.3: Recording Process
This class covers how accounts, debits and credits are used to record business transactions. This class also covers how a journal, ledger and posting are used and how a trial balance is prepared.
4:
Class No.4: Adjusting Accounts
This class covers the concept of the accrual basis of accounting and adjusting entries to create accrual and deferral accounts. After completing an adjusted trial balance, you learn how financial statements are prepared.
5:
Class No.5: Closing Accounts
With the closing process, an accounting cycle is completed. The closing process includes journalizing and posting closing entries and preparation of post-closing trial balance.
6:
Class No.6: Accounting for Merchandising Operations
In this class, an accounting cycle for merchandsing operations is presented. It includes how revenues and expenses are recorded, how inventories are maintained and how an income statement is prepared.
7:
Class No.7: Inventories
This class covers the classification of inventories and how cost flow assumptions affect financial statements. This class also covers presentation of inventories and how they affect financial statements.
8:
Class No.8: Internal Control
Sound accounting practice requires an adequate system of internal control being placed in. This class covers the basic elements of internal control and how they are applied.
9:
Class No.9: Accounting for Receivables
This class covers how a company recognizes and clears receivable accounts, including the types of receivables and how interest is accrued, as well as presentation and analysis of receivables.
10:
Class No.10: Tangible and Intangible Assets
This class covers accounting for tangible and intangible assets such as land, buildings, and machinery, including depreciation methods, impairment, and retirement.
11:
Class No.11: Liabilities
In this class, accounting for current and long-term liabilities is discussed, including the types of liabilities and how they are accounted for, as well as how they are presented and analyzed.
12:
Class No.12 Stockholders' Equity
This class focuses on a corporation, or a stock company, to depict how equity works and to understand the components of equity. The class also covers how equity transactions are accounted for and how equity accounts are presented and analyzed.
13:
Class No.13: Statement of Cash Flows
This class covers the usefulness of the statement of cash flows and how cash flows are classified. The class also covers how the statement of cash flows is prepared.
14:
Class No.14: Financial Statement Analysis / Time Value of Money
This class covers how financial statements are used in various analyses, as well as how a company's performance is analyzed using ratio analyses. This class also introduces the concept of the time value of money.

subtitle: Historical Roots and Modern Pathways of Russian Economy
summary: This course offers a comprehensive examination ofthe Russian economy across historical and contemporary contexts. Beginning withthe foundations of Tsarist and Soviet economic development, it traces thetransition to a market economy after 1991, explores centre–region dynamics, andanalyses Russia’s economic model prior to 2022. The course concludes with anin‑depth study of the impact of sanctions imposed after 2014 and 2022,highlighting structural adaptation, financial isolation, and Russia’s geoeconomicreorientation. Students will engage in written and oral assignments, combininghistorical analysis with contemporary policy evaluation.
goal:
The objectives of the course are:
• To provide students with a structured understanding of Russia’s economic development from the Tsarist period to the present.
• To analyse the political economy of Soviet industrialisation, post‑Soviet transition reforms, and regional economic specialisation.
• To evaluate Russia’s foreign economic relations and the challenges of diversification prior to 2022.
• To critically assess the scope, intent, and consequences of sanctions regimes and Russia’s adaptive strategies.
• To develop skills in academic writing, comparative analysis, and oral presentation within the field of international political economy.
By the end of the course, students will be able to:
• Explain the historical trajectory of Russia’s economic development, including Soviet and post‑Soviet phases.
•Analyse the institutional and policy frameworks shaping Russia’s transition to a market economy.
• Evaluate the role of regional economic specialisation and policy in shaping centre–region relations.
• Assess Russia’s pre‑2022 economic model, including resource dependence and diversification attempts.
• Critically compare the sanctions regimes of 2014 and 2022, identifying their economic and geopolitical implications.
• Apply academic writing conventions in short essays supported by references and bibliographies.
• Present research findings clearly and persuasively in both individual and group formats.
• Reflect on the long‑term outlook for Russia’s economy under sanctions within a global comparative perspective.
study_outside:
Students are expected to demonstrate a genuine interest in Russian studies and a commitment to understanding the evolution of Russia’s socio‑economic model. While no prior background in economics is strictly required, familiarity with basic economic concepts will be advantageous for engaging with the course material.

During the course, you are required to submit Exit Tickets (two‑sentence summarising memos) for the specified sessions. Essays must be properly referenced and accompanied by a Bibliography (not included in the word count). A template and evaluation criteria are posted on Moodle. name: Fiscal Policy: on Taxation and Well-being　51
summary_excerpt: Our class aims to understand the theory and practice of taxation and well-......
summary:
Our class aims to understand the theory and practice of taxation and well-being. We highly emphasize the criteria of efficiency and equity. Considering these two criteria, the course consists of three parts after explaining the features of tax systems in Japan.
Part one presents the construction of a theoretical framework for taxation and income distribution, which is closely related to equity criterion. We analyze tax incidence on commodities and production factors, and discuss commodity taxation without competition.
Part two deals with the topics on taxation and efficiency. Main issues in Part two include tax incidence, excess burden with indifference curves and demand curves. These issues can be revisited as welfare costs of taxation at partial and general equilibrium analysis.
Part three constructs a basic economic model for analyzing efficient and equitable taxation. Two important topics in Part three are optimal commodity taxation and optimal income taxation. We study some rules on commodity tax design such as the Ramsey rule and the Corlett-Hague rule covering optimal commodity taxation. Optimal income taxation can be classified as optimal linear and nonlinear income tax. We also mention a critique of normative optimal taxation and empirical evidence of positive optimal taxation.
Thisclass will be conducted by face-to-face. I will provide lecture notes andlecture materials through the [Announcement] on the class of [Fiscal Issueson Social Security
01] inadvance (maybe late September or early October).
goal: This course focuses on making students understand theory and practice related to the criteria of efficiency and equity. We recommend that students grasp the main features of Japanese tax systems in in practical side, and that they study how taxes distort the market, how government intervenes market failures and it designs commodity and income taxes.

Hence, students should recognize that some math (like calculus) in this course is required while the necessary math is explained during the lectures. This advanced seminar reads and discusses the theory and policy of economic development. The key concepts to be reviewed include poverty and inequality, growth, human security and institutions. Our approach is interdisciplinary and students learn to evaluate development policies both quantitatively and qualitatively. Students will conduct a primary data survey (in compliance with University policies regarding the field trips) to complete a graduation thesis, using statistics / econometrics software (STATA) and a strong inter-cultural communication skills are required (the second foreign language other than English is a plus). Students learn to set up and prove working hypothesis and draw feasible policy recommendations for real issues. In the past, students participated field trips to the Philippines, India, Indonesia, East Timor, China and Cambodia. Students are expected to take or have taken Economic Development offered by the same instructor in Fall semester.

subtitle: Game Theory & Mechanism Design
summary:
This seminar aims to provide students with the knowledge and background necessary
to understand cutting-edge research in theoretical economics, particularly in game theory and mechanism design
. In recent years, game theory and mechanism design have been increasingly applied in various societal contexts, including recommendation systems, auction design, school choice mechanisms, and so on.
For successful social implementation, it is essential to have a solid theoretical foundation that enables a precise understanding of these mechanisms. In particular, without a rigorous mathematical approach, such theories cannot adequately address the risks and complexities that arise in real-world applications. Consequently,
all papers read in the seminar will be mathematically formulated literature only
. Students are expected to approach the seminar with sufficient motivation to engage with such an approach.
This seminar focuses on developing students’ ability to understand the mathematical models underlying these social implementations, as well as their capacity to apply these models to create new theoretical frameworks, through systematic study of the mathematical foundations of game theory and mechanism design.
goal: The seminar aims to equip students with the fundamental knowledge required to read cutting-edge research papers in game theory and mechanism design, as well as with the ability to understand how to approach academic papers and develop their own ideas based on them. In particular, students who write their graduation theses within this seminar are required to conduct surveys of specialized academic literature. Accordingly, the seminar places strong emphasis on cultivating the ability to independently carry out rigorous literature surveys and synthesize existing research.
study_outside:
To achieve the objectives described above, this seminar will devote little time to textbook-level explanations. While extensive prior knowledge is not strictly required, students are expected to independently review and supplement any foundational material they lack through self-study. The level of the seminar substantially extends the content of the instructor’s courses, Behavioral & Experimental Game Theory and Mechanism Design in Practice; therefore, a solid understanding of these courses is considered essential.
In addition, the seminar frequently holds
joint research seminars with the School of Engineering at the University of Tokyo
. Students are expected to actively participate in these collaborative research activities and to demonstrate a strong motivation to acquire deep and specialized expertise.
Preview and Review may take around 90-120 min. each.

The goal of this advanced seminar series is to foster students’ creative confidence, design and visual literacy, and understanding of the distinct business challenges in industries in which creativity, sensibility, the consumer experience and cultural resonance are key. The transformation of enterprises and work is accelerating with digitisation and Ai, disrupting industries and once-stable career paths. Under the general rubric of ‘Creative Industries’, it has the following three semester sub-themes, in this order: Creative by Design (Fall I), Selling Sensibility (Spring I), and The Design Enterprise (Fall III).

subtitle: Selected Topics in Decarbonisation Studies and Sustainable Development Research
summary:
This seminar brings together students interested in exploring critical issues at the intersection of global decarbonisation efforts and sustainable development research. Adopting a “selected topics” approach, the course invites students to engage with contemporary challenges, innovative solutions, policy frameworks, and the socio‑economic dimensions of the transition to a low‑carbon and sustainable future. Emphasis is placed on critical analysis, interdisciplinary perspectives, and the integration of theoretical and empirical scholarship.
Schematically, the keyareas for individual research in this Seminar can be introduced as follows:
1. Decarbonisation inSpecific Sectors
1.1 Energy
• Renewable energyintegration: Examines the incorporation of solar, wind, and geothermaltechnologies into existing power grids, alongside energy storage solutions andsmart grid systems.
• Decarbonising heat andelectricity: Explores the electrification of heating systems, the developmentof efficient heating technologies, and optimisation of energy consumption inbuildings.
• Fossil fuel transition:Investigates pathways for phasing out fossil fuels, including carbon captureand storage (CCS) technologies and the development of alternative fuels.
• Smart energy systems:Focuses on optimising energy production, distribution, and consumption throughintelligent technologies and data analytics.
1.2 Transportation
• Electrification ofvehicles: Studies the development of electric vehicles, charginginfrastructure, and integration into the power grid.
• Alternative fuels:Explores the use of biofuels, hydrogen, and other sustainable fuel sources fortransportation.
• Sustainable urbanmobility: Investigates strategies for promoting public transport, cycling, andwalking, as well as optimising logistics and freight systems.
1.3 Buildings andConstruction
• Energy efficiency inbuildings: Focuses on improving insulation, optimising heating and coolingsystems, and promoting energy‑efficient appliances.
• Sustainable buildingmaterials: Examines the use of recycled and renewable materials in constructionand strategies to reduce the carbon footprint of building materials.
• Retrofitting andrenovation: Investigates approaches to improving the energy efficiency ofexisting buildings through retrofitting and renovation.
1.4 Industry
• Industrialelectrification: Explores the use of electricity to power industrial processes,replacing fossil fuel‑based technologies.
• Carbon capture,storage, and utilisation (CCSU): Focuses on capturing carbon dioxide emissionsfrom industrial processes and utilising them in products such as chemicals orfuels.
• Process optimisation:Examines methods for reducing energy consumption and emissions through improvedindustrial processes.
2. Sustainable EconomicDevelopment
• Circular economy:Explores principles of waste reduction, resource efficiency, and materialsrecovery across sectors.
• Sustainable consumptionand production: Promotes sustainable consumption patterns, reduced waste, andoptimised resource use.
• Ecosystem restoration:Focuses on restoring degraded ecosystems, protecting biodiversity, andenhancing ecosystem services.
• Environmental policyand governance: Examines policies and regulations supporting decarbonisationand sustainable development, including carbon pricing, emissions tradingsystems (ETS), and green finance.
• Social equity andjustice: Considers climate litigation and activism, the social implications ofdecarbonisation, and strategies to ensure a just and equitable transition to alow‑carbon economy.
3. Policy and Governance
• Climate changemitigation and adaptation: Studies international climate agreements (e.g. ParisAgreement mechanisms), climate impacts, and strategies for reducing greenhousegas emissions and adapting to climate change.
• Place‑baseddecarbonisation: Explores the role of sub‑national and local governance, withstrategies tailored to specific geographic locations and industrial clusters.
• Geopolitics ofdecarbonisation: Analyses the geopolitical consequences of transitioning to alow‑carbon economy.
goal: Course Objectives
study_outside:
Prerequisites and Course Organisation
An acquaintance with macroeconomics, the elements of economic analysis, and statistics is advantageous for this course. Prior completion of courses in economic development, the political economy of development, or related disciplines may also be helpful. Above all, a genuine aspiration to deepen understanding of the topics outlined is essential.
This is an interactive seminar. Enrolment requires regular preparation for sessions and active engagement in class activities. Sessions are typically convened with the instructor acting as a discussant and moderator. Students are expected to read both assigned and self‑selected materials in advance and to prepare commentaries and questions for in‑class discussion.
Reading materials, including academic publications, will be selected collaboratively by the instructor and students, depending on the academic interests of the participants. Materials will be recommended at least one week prior to each session. Students are encouraged to suggest resources relevant to their course paper or thesis work.
Each student will deliver two individual presentations: an introduction of their chosen theme at the beginning of the course, and a presentation of the revised version of their research at the end of the semester. To assist with preparation, a template outlining the core elements of a research project will be distributed via Moodle.
Students should also be prepared to reflect on assigned readings during regular sessions. To enable fruitful collaboration, participants are expected to forward to the instructor their prepared notes, commentaries, or questions on the assigned readings or other materials studied for the specified sessions. (The number of such sessions may vary depending on enrolment.)
The ultimate goal of the course is the production of a course paper, with the prospect of elaborating it into a senior thesis in the final semester. Work on the course paper is organised in three components:
• Individual: presentations, reflections on readings, and writing.
• Pair: peer‑reviewing of course paper drafts and commenting on second‑round presentations towards the end of the semester.
• Group: broader discussions in class.
Students in their final semester will prepare and present their senior theses.

name: Introduction to Architecture
teacher: ゴラニ　ソロモン　エレズ
summary_excerpt: Throughout the twentieth century, the architecture of the house has been a......
subtitle: The Japanese House Studio
summary:
Throughout the twentieth century, the architecture of the house has been a locus for experimentation with ideas about ways of living, individual expression, and social relation and class. It served as a platform of design trialing for materials and forms and was the site where architects have sought to offer new domestic lifestyles. From Kenzo Tange and Kazuo Shinohara to Sou Fujimoto and Atelier Bow-Wow, nearly all architects of the past hundred years have catalyzed their most elaborated ideas through the design of houses. The house is not simply one type within the architectural vast constructed inventory, but arguably the most important medium for the investigation of architectural ideas.
Our window into the field of architecture will be a small, carefully selected group of seminal houses, which were constructed in Japan from the beginning of the 20th Century until the last decade. These works of architecture have an accumulated value. Each of them had the ability to mirror a crystallized image of its social-cultural-political surroundings at the time of construction and carries extraordinary relevance to the study of the field even today. As a group they form a balanced account of architectural traditions in the modern period and an opportunity for acquaintance with the architectural knowledge of that time, drawing from a range of fields that influence how a building is designed, described, constructed, with how it is imagined and with how it is used once build.
The course will be conducted in a form of a studio. Each of the participating students will be assigned to one project/house. The work during the semester will occur along two paths. In the first, students will conduct a study in relation to ‘their’ particular house, gather material for a ‘box of references’, and gain an understanding of its architectural style, its use and structure, its motivation, and contextual power. At the second path of the course, we will study through practice. In this section each student will construct a series of physical, analytical models of his/her assigned house, getting familiar with design ideas, understanding spatial concerns, considering methods and materials, and offering individual interpretations.
The course has no prerequisites. Besides an interest in the course subjects, students are not required to have any prior knowledge of architecture. There will be no writing assignment. The course will conclude in a presentation and in an exhibition of the models.
goal: Acquiring knowledge of central concepts in the field of architecture, and establishing complex connections between those concepts through acts of analysis and representation.

summary: In translation practices, students have to show advanced Japanese language skills; just being a native Japanese speaker is not enough to do translation. When you register, you need to know your Japanese language proficiency; if language skill is not enough, you should realize you will not be able to get grades you expect. This course will focus on practices in translating short English texts (up to two pages) from various genres into Japanese. Translation consists in reproducing the reception language to the closest natural equivalent of the source-language message, first in terms of meaning and secondly in terms of style. Though style is secondary to contents, it is nevertheless important. We should not translate poetry as though it were prose, nor essay as though it were expository material. A translation should preserve somewhat the beauty of style and the flowing cadences of the original. Therefore, the important thing is to be able to build a Japanese translation so that those who have not read the English original(poems, proses, and essays)might enjoy. To do so, many skills and considerable background knowledge should be accumulated. In this course, the following points will be dealt with: skills such as how to consult dictionaries, to write persuasive Japanese, to interpret literary texts, and to acquire a great deal of knowledge of British and American culture, society and literature. Through classroom discussions, we will find ways to improve translated versions that students might create. For this purpose, regular attendance, participation and adequate reading/writing (understanding) proficiencies in Japanese are required.
goal:
The aim of this course is for the student to be able to create an accurate and reliable Japanese version on the basis of the translation rules they might learn each week; Students will learn various ‘styles’.
Translating literary texts should be more about the creative imagination than it is about the rule-governed text analysis. The translator should be more like a poet or a novelist than like a machine translation system.

subtitle: Rereading the literature of Japanese Empire in the Anthropocene
summary:
Human civiilation develped within the 10,000-year period known as the Holocene during which the processes that regulate the stability and resilience of the Earth system were remarkably stable. Now, however, human behavior has begun to push such processes beyond their ability to recover, threatening to destabalize them with catastrophic consequences. Although like many institutions around the world, Japanese universites refuse to acknowldge this crisis, as students educate themselves, they increasingly realize that they are facing an unprecedented climate and ecological emergency that will not be solved by better technology. One goal of this course is to create space for young people to share their concerns for the future.
Japanese Translation for the purposes of this course does not presuppose only linguistic translation, but includes as well the social and cultural appropriation of Western-centered modernity, which involved radically new ways of organizing knowledge. The creation of the modern nation-state requires the “invention of tradition,” made possible through the reformulation of older cultural productions. From the Meiji period onward, literature may thus be read as a double translation of Western modernity and pre-Meiji cultural forms. Literary translation plays a central role in the construction of modern Japanese language (kokugo) and modern national literature. We will deconstruct the idea of national culture as we embark on close readings of Japanese modern literature.
This is a student-centered course in which students consider relations among language, culture, gender, race/ethnicity, power, nation and empire. Students interested in participating enthusiastically in a classroom community that emphasizes ethical and social engagement are especially welcome.
goal: This course should give students a greater understanding of Japanese history, Japanese literature, and postcolonial and gender theory. The class is designed to help students rethink institutions and systems of knowledge created within modernity. Engaged students are also given guided opportunities to develop skills in critical reading, writing, self-expression, analytical reasoning, social engagement, communication and community building.

summary: In this advanced course, we will explore Shakespeare’s plays alongside their film adaptations, examining not only the rich and complex worlds of Shakespeare’s texts but also the dynamic and exciting interaction between literature and its visual adaptations. Through analysis of Shakespeare’s plays and film screenings, we will discuss how Shakespeare’s plays were shaped by the cultural and social contexts of his time and how Shakespearean adaptations have also been shaped by the cultural and social contexts of the time of their production and reception. By focusing, for example, on critical debates surrounding feminism, gender and race, we will explore how film adaptations of Shakespeare’s plays have been deeply influenced by our shifting perspectives on these themes and by the emerging cultural and social movements of the twentieth and twenty-first centuries. Each week, we will focus on one Shakespearean play and its significant film adaptations and discuss the nuanced and often innovative ways in which Shakespeare’s timeless texts have been read by scholars, readers, theatre practitioners and filmmakers and reimagined through adaptation.

subtitle: TOKYO － Out of the Ordinary
summary:
The course aims to introduce what is arguably the most complex product of society and Japanese society in particular — the city, and to concentrate on the city of Tokyo.
Our study will encompass a range of issues concerning the city, and the complex consequences of urban developments under modern and contemporary conditions. We will observe how the city has defined, and was in itself defined by, a particular reality at a particular time, beginning in Edo period and concluding in the present. Such an approach emphasizes a need to examine the external relations of the city with context, and particularly relate to its social, cultural and political circumstances. Thus, we will look at the creation and recreation of the city’s physical texture, at architecture, urban landscape, infrastructure and technology, and at the same time observe the city as a social product determined by everyday life and habitual practices, organization of the immediate surrounding, personal rites and the micro-politics of life in the city. In the same manner, we will look at buildings and neighborhoods per se, as a material construct guided by geometry and legal code, but at the same time recognize how the pragmatics of this built environment interrelate with cultural systems such as literature and film, and thus examine the mechanisms that relate the city to culture. Also, we will see how the city is not merely a reflection or expression of politics, but rather an intricate political apparatus in and of itself, influencing relationships and encouraging change.
There are two consecutive class sessions every week. Usually, there will be a lecture at the first session, and the second lecture period will be used for class discussions, screening of films and videos, visiting lectures, or field trips. In taking the classroom outside the campus, we will use the benefit of the Tokyo locality to be in and see the subjects of our study. These activities are equally important to the class lectures and should be used to further practice critical thinking and develop skills for analyzing the built city.
The course has no prerequisites. Besides an interest in the course’s subjects, students are not required to have any prior knowledge of Tokyo, architecture, art and/or other disciplines of urban studies.
goal: As a whole, the course aims to discuss central themes emerging from the city of Tokyo. It aims to acquaint students with detailed knowledge about the modern and contemporary histories of the city, and an ability to position this knowledge in a range of discursive and theoretical frameworks.

summary:
a. Face-to-Face (F2F)
It is said that all humans have an innate desire to imitate and copy their environment—a concept known as the “dramatic instinct.” When this instinct is fully engaged, drama becomes a highly effective and natural means of learning. Through processes such as imitation, interpretation, imagination, and role-playing, much of a child’s learning in language, logical thinking, movement, and social behavior takes place.
“Drama in Education” is also a dynamic learning experience that caters to a broad range of students with diverse intelligences and prepares them for effective and responsible participation in society. It is now recognized as a crucial subject that supplements the limitations of conventional IQ-based learning.
Course Organization
During the first four weeks, you will be exposed to a wide range of readings as well as various drama techniques and methodologies to prepare you for the design, implementation, and evaluation of drama activities. After these initial four weeks, each group will report on an assigned drama practitioner and conduct a drama activity based on a lesson plan your group has created. The entire class will then reflect on the activity at the end of the session. (For detailed information on projects, please refer to “Project Procedures.”) Additionally, each group will report on Dr. Shoyo Tsubouchi’s work on child drama activities, based on the assigned paper.

subtitle: WRITING, READING, & EDITING CREATIVE NONFICTION
summary:
Creative nonfiction is one of the most prevalent modes of discourse in the 21st century. It is everywhere from literary magazines to newspapers, books, blogs and websites. In this course, students will read, write, and investigate an array of creative nonfiction writing such as personal narrative/memoir, profile, essays on popular culture, and the lyric essay. Students will read a diverse range of works from various national traditions for their craft and technique. This course will expose students to read and write in forms ranging from popular, literary, and experimental. Some of the authors we will read are: Zadie Smith, Maggie Nelson, Rebecca Brown, Eula Biss, Hanif Abdurraqib, Jenny Zhang, Virginia Woolf and others. Students will learn the core elements of prose writing: voice, scene, description, and structure. The final portfolio will consist of three original revised essays or a video essay.
This is an advanced course where students will be required to engage in combination of writing exercises (including collaborative exercises),
class discussions (of assigned readings) and workshops. The writing workshop--where you will be asked to provide detailed and constructive feedback on peer work--will be a central component of the course.
By the end of the course you will have produced a significant body of writing in the form of:
1) three revised essays of around 2,500 words
2) various drafts of the following essays: personal narrative, pop culture, and lyric essay
3) written responses to weekly assignments. Approx. 500 words
4) written responses to peer work: Approx. 800 words
5) other writing generated through exercises assigned in-class
The average length of weekly reading assignments (essays) will be between 10,000 to 20,000 words and there will be an additional 3,000 to 6,000 words of peer work to read on workshop weeks. This means that on a busy week you may have more than 25,000 words of reading and 3,000 words of writing (essays, peer feed-back,reading responses, etc.).
While there is no prerequisite for this course, given the workload and strict emphasis on attendance/participation, this advanced course is recommended for students who:
1) have previously taken creative writing and/or literature courses at the university level
2) are capable of handling reading assignments of significant length in English
3) enjoy actively participating in and leading group work and class discussions
4) are able to work in an organized manner (including submitting weekly assignments beforehand via Moodle)
5) enjoy thinking/writing both creatively and analytically) and already have ideas about writing that they would like to pursue as part of the course
6) students will be required to work collaboratively and critically with classmates on a weekly basis
The expectation is that students will attend every class and submit all assignments.

summary:
This course combines weekly lectures with student-led discussions and presentations exploring the translation, production, and reception of Japanese literature in the Anglosphere in the twenty-first century.
As the course focuses on a specialized topic, it is best suited to students with some prior knowledge of Japanese and/or international literature, as well as an interest in literary translation, cross-cultural exchange, publishing, and the historical and sociological dimensions of literary production.
The course will be conducted in both Japanese and English. Students should be able to (1) follow lectures in both languages and (2) complete substantial reading assignments in Japanese and English, although most theoretical readings will be provided in English. Students are welcome to participate in either Japanese or English, whichever they feel best enables them to express their ideas. They should also be comfortable engaging in discussions in which classmates may use either language.
Those interested in an interactive, workshop-based class focusing on the practice of literary translation may find that my course Translation as Creative Writing is a better fit. Other students may be interested in pairing the two classes so that they have both a content-focused class and a more interactive practice-focused class. SILS also offers a range of compelling literature/translation courses by other instructors on topics ranging from Modern Japanese Literature, postcolonial literature and the theory of translation.

Please submit assignment in the following format:

* Font 11 or 12 (in Times New Roman, Arial or another reader-friendly font)
* 1.5 or double-space
* Include your name at the top of the first page and page numbers at bottom of all pages.
* Leave 25 mm margins on top and bottom, and 20 mm margins on left and right (so that your classmates can make notes directly onto the printed copy).
* You can choose to print-out copies either single-sided.
* Staple pages together at the top left-hand corner.

In this workshop students are asked to produce works of short fiction or translation of around 2500~3000 words. While no set topic or theme will be assigned, please keep the following in mind when writing stories for workshops.

In this class students are asked to provide feedback

* by hand in the margins of the printed copies of stories

subtitle: Reading and Discussing English Literature
summary:
In this advanced seminar, we will explore William Shakespeare’s
Romeo and Juliet
through close reading/dramatic reading, discussion and critical analysis. You will be divided into small groups to read and discuss, sharing your thoughts on the scene(s) and the characters. The instructor will also provide critical analysis of the play and encourage you to develop your own interpretations. When time permits, we will also watch TV and film adaptations of the play to enrich our understanding of the enduring relevance of Shakespeare’s text.
This seminar is built around active participation and designed to be collaborative and lively—a safe space where students can test out ideas, ask questions and experience Shakespeare’s play from multiple angles.
Alongside the readings and discussions, you will also learn how to write an academic essay to effectively communicate your interpretation of the text. In the latter half of the course, you are encouraged to think about your forthcoming graduation thesis project by coming up with possible topics you would like to work on.
Please also read my section in the “Advanced Seminar Course List and Information, Fall 2026.”

summary:

The course is designed to provide students with the ability to understand and use basic statistical concepts and methods. The beginning of the course explores statistical data summaries, data organization, and how to draw conclusions from data. Additional topics covered include random variables, least-squares regression line, probability rules, point estimation and confidence intervals.
goal: By the end of the semester students should be able to meet the following objectives:

data.

Measures of variability.
(w3) (2.3) Understanding and interpreting the standard deviation, (2.4) Measures of relative
standing.
(w4) (3) Introduction, (3.2) Describing bivariate quantitative data.

simple events.

probabilities.
(w7) (5.1) Discrete random variables and their probability distributions, (5.2) The binomial
probability distribution.
(w8) (5.2) The binomial probability distribution (finish), (6.1) Probability distributions for
continuous random variables.
(w9) (6.1) Probability distributions for continuous random variables (finish), (6.2) The normal
probability distribution.
(w10) (7) Introduction, (7.2) Statistics and sampling distributions, (7.3) The central limit theorem
and the sample mean (including: The central limit theorem).

of the sample proportion.

(w15) Final exam.

summary:
IMPORTANT: This course will be taught Face-To-Face.
This course offers an introductory, literacy-levelapproach to data science, designed with no prerequisites in programming orcalculus. However, students are expected to have completed either "GE122Introductory Statistics A" or "GE123 Introductory Statistics B."Students will develop a foundational understanding of data science, focusing onkey concepts, tools, and practical applications. Students will learn essential conceptsand techniques for data collection, cleaning, and visualization to drawinsights from diverse datasets. Key machine learning methods, includingregression, classification, clustering, and dimensionality reduction, will beintroduced, with Python integrated for hands-on practice. Students will alsoexplore advanced topics such as natural language processing, image and audioprocessing, and an introduction to reinforcement learning and deep learning.Additionally, students will examine the ethical considerations in data science,including algorithmic biases, data privacy, and related issues.
goal:
In this course, students will:
* Learn foundational concepts of data science, including its scope, applications, and basic tools.
* Learn techniques for data collection, cleaning, and preparation to ensure data quality and reliability.
* Learn methods for effective data visualization to communicate insights from various datasets.
* Learn key machine learning techniques, such as regression, classification, clustering, and dimensionality reduction.
* Gain hands-on experience with Python for implementing data science methods and models.
* Explore advanced topics, including natural language processing, image and audio processing.
* Examine ethical considerations in data science, such as algorithmic biases, data privacy.
study_outside:
* Pre-lecture preparation: Review the assigned textbook sections for each week to familiarize yourself with the upcoming topics and key concepts.
* Post-lecture reinforcement: Solidify your understanding of lecture content by revisiting the relevant textbook sections. Complete assignments to apply and deepen your grasp of the material.
As part of your preparation, you will be asked to read the handouts for each session that will be posted on Waseda Moodle in advance. Preparation is expected to take 90-120 minutes. Homework will be assigned as review for each class and should be turned in before the next class. The review is expected to take 90-120 minutes.
schedule_plan:
1:
Vol. 1 Introduction to Data Science
Overviewof data science, course structure, data science in real world, and briefoverview of prior knowledge from high school 'Information Studies'.
2:
Vol. 2 Categorizing and Collecting Data
ExploringDiverse Data Types: Introduction to text, image, and audio processing, dataobtained through web, experiment, survey, etc.
3:
Vol. 3 Summarizing and Visualizing Data
VisualizingData for Insight: Learn techniques for creating tables, charts, and exploringmean, deviation, percentile, standardization, etc.
4:
Vol. 4 Interpreting and Analyzing Data Using Introductory Methods
Basicsfor Analysis using Data: Exploring correlation versus causation, level versusrate of change, and learning how to interpret decomposition, regression, PCA,etc.
5:
Vol. 5 Persuasive Data Analysis
PresentingAnalysis Effectively: Understand the process of defining research questions,forming testable hypotheses, and using presentation tools (Word, PowerPoint,Tex) to clearly communicate your findings.
6:
Vol. 6 Introduction to Data Science Tools: Part 1
PythonBasics: Introduction to Python programming for data handling and analysis.
7:
Vol. 7 Introduction to Data Science Tools: Part 2
PythonBasics: Introduction to Python programming for data handling and analysis.
8:
Vol. 8 Machine Learning & AI: Part 1
CoreML Techniques: Introduction to machine learning and AI, regression,classification, clustering, and dimensionality reduction.
9:
Vol. 9 Machine Learning & AI : Part 2
CoreML Techniques: Introduction to decision trees, ensemble learning, reinforcementlearning, deep learning, and interpretability techniques (e.g., SHAP, LIME).
10:
Vol.10 Text Analysis Techniques: Part 1
Introductionto NLP: Learn basic methods and applications of natural language processing(NLP).
11:
Vol.11 Text Analysis Techniques : Part 2
Introductionto NLP: Learn basic methods and applications of natural language processing(NLP).
12:
Vol.12 Image and Audio Processing
Introductionto image and audio processing methods for data science applications.
13:
Vol.13 Ethical and Future Implications of Data Science
DataEthics and Limitations: Discuss ethics, biases, accountability, datagovernance, and the limitations of data science.
14:
Vol.14 Final Exam
Finalexamination, and feedback via Waseda Moodle

summary:
IMPORTANT: This course will be taught Face-To-Face.
This course offers an introductory, literacy-levelapproach to data science, designed with no prerequisites in programming orcalculus. However, students are expected to have completed either "GE122Introductory Statistics A" or "GE123 Introductory Statistics B."Students will develop a foundational understanding of data science, focusing onkey concepts, tools, and practical applications. Students will learn essential conceptsand techniques for data collection, cleaning, and visualization to drawinsights from diverse datasets. Key machine learning methods, includingregression, classification, clustering, and dimensionality reduction, will beintroduced, with Python integrated for hands-on practice. Students will alsoexplore advanced topics such as natural language processing, image and audioprocessing, and an introduction to reinforcement learning and deep learning.Additionally, students will examine the ethical considerations in data science,including algorithmic biases, data privacy, and related issues.
goal:
In this course, students will:
* Learn foundational concepts of data science, including its scope, applications, and basic tools.
* Learn techniques for data collection, cleaning, and preparation to ensure data quality and reliability.
* Learn methods for effective data visualization to communicate insights from various datasets.
* Learn key machine learning techniques, such as regression, classification, clustering, and dimensionality reduction.
* Gain hands-on experience with Python for implementing data science methods and models.
* Explore advanced topics, including natural language processing, image and audio processing.
* Examine ethical considerations in data science, such as algorithmic biases, data privacy.
study_outside:
* Pre-lecture preparation: Review the assigned textbook sections for each week to familiarize yourself with the upcoming topics and key concepts.
* Post-lecture reinforcement: Solidify your understanding of lecture content by revisiting the relevant textbook sections. Complete assignments to apply and deepen your grasp of the material.
As part of your preparation, you will be asked to read the handouts for each session that will be posted on Waseda Moodle in advance. Preparation is expected to take 90-120 minutes. Homework will be assigned as review for each class and should be turned in before the next class. The review is expected to take 90-120 minutes.

subtitle: The Story of Kimono: Fashion and Tradition
summary:
This seminar explores the history of kimono with a particular focus on its development in the Edo period. Through reading scholarly texts and analyzing visual and textual sources, students will study the history of kimono and examine how clothing and fashion illustrate societal, economic, and cultural characteristics of the time.
Class sessions will mainly consist of discussions and presentations based on assigned readings. Students will be required to give short presentations about the reading, a particular item (kimono or image of kimono), or a particular topic related to the history of kimono (technology, event, person, etc.). The number and format of the presentations will depend on the class size. If possible, we may also have one or two field trips to observe the textile traditions. Towards the end of the semester, students will work on an essay project.
goal: 1) Students have improved knowledge of the history and culture of Japan.
study_outside:
1) Students are expected to read the assigned readings thoroughly before class and to be prepared to discuss them. There will be assignments to guide their preparation and students are required to complete them before each class. These assignments will be used as discussion materials and shared with other students. This will take 60-120 minutes.
2) Students will make presentations, which will require 5-10 hours each. The number of presentations will depend on the size of the class.
3) Students will write a ﬁnal essay, which should require more than 20 hours to complete.

subtitle: Bringing Classical Theatre to Life: A Performance Reading Workshop
summary:
Discover how classical plays come alive through voice — revealing new narratives through performance
Experience masterpieces from Shakespeare to Beckett and Mishima Yukio, not through silent reading alone, but through vocal performance and dramatic reading. By embodying the emotions, struggles, and joys of characters through voice, participants will discover new dimensions of dramatic works that remain hidden in text alone.
Experience masterpieces from Shakespeare to Beckett and Mishima Yukio, not through silent reading alone, but through vocal performance and dramatic reading. By embodying the emotions, struggles, and joys of characters through voice, participants will discover new dimensions of dramatic works that remain hidden in text alone.
For each work, we'll begin with historical context and theatrical significance, followed by group readings where participants take turns playing different roles. Our post-reading discussions will explore the deeper layers of each work that become apparent only through performance, and we'll examine the unique expressive possibilities that theatre offers. No prior theatrical experience is necessary. Join us in exploring new ways of reading and enjoying classical theatre.

name: First Year Seminar B　55
teacher: ドボルザーク　グレッグ
summary_excerpt: We often use the words “mainstream,” “normal,” or “everyday,” without cons......
subtitle: Inequalities and Intersections: Transnational Gender and Culture in the Margins
summary:
We often use the words “mainstream,” “normal,” or “everyday,” without considering the inherent violence behind the idea of privileging some people as normal and considering some as “different,” “other,” or otherwise marginal. What are the dynamics of this process of othering, who benefits, and who suffers? Whole populations of people have been marginalized by war, colonialism, and militarism. Whole groups of people have been marginalized by ideas about what is considered an “abnormal” identity. How can one better appreciate the diversity and complexity of humanity by taking historical account of this violence and inequality?
This first-year seminar is part of a series of seminars that applies cultural studies and gender studies approaches to the postcolonial history and present-day of the Asia and Pacific region, challenging students to think about colonized, displaced, and marginalized communities and subjects in different societies. Considering ideas about citizenship/borders, immigration, indigenous communities (like Ainu or Okinawan), Disney movies and popular cultural ideas about gender, sexual orientation and human rights, race, and other keywords, we think about how all these different themes intersect. We also give some consideration to how those keywords relate to marginalized, colonized regions like Hawai'i, Okinawa, and the colonized Pacific Islands, with a particular emphasis of the place where we are doing this study-- the place we call "Japan."
goal: By taking an assertive, participant, self-reflexive approach, students in this seminar shall develop a basic understanding of problems of nationalism, ethnicity, gender, and popular culture, with a particular emphasis on how these issues relate to the Asia and Pacific region between Japan and the United States. Students will conduct group presentations and each write a short analytic piece related to how these themes intersect a subject of their choosing. They will also be encouraged to cultivate a nuanced awareness of this region, the societies in which they live, and the complexity of their own lives.
study_outside: You will be required to read the assigned readings posted to Moodle or watch certain videos, etc. prior to each class and be prepared for active discussion every single time. Preview and Review may take around 90-120 min. each at least.
schedule_plan:
This is a two-credit seminar course which will meet once a week both in person (and, if necessary, online) for one period, in principle. Since in-person engagement is so important, unless there is a university guideline to completely study online, we will give preference to classroom time only, meaning that if you're feeling sick, it's best that you stay home and get excused from class entirely and do a catch-up assignment later rather than asking for a special hybrid setup, which can be quite distracting to the class.
Topics will cover themes of gender, ethnicity, race, colonialism, power, and other issues of interest to students (based on a survey at the beginning of class). We will construct the course schedule together around student presentations, readings, and activities. There is no test for this course, but you will be required to do readings every week and to prepare substantially for every session. summary_excerpt: In order to make decisions about our present actions and to plan for the f......
subtitle: Informing ourselves through news reports
summary:
In order to make decisions about our present actions and to plan for the future, it’s important to have knowledge of what is happening in the world around us. Yet the teacher of this class has found that many students do not keep up with the news. In this class, we will read about, analyze and discuss current aﬀairs as presented through English-language news sources. We'll discuss both the issues themselves as well as how they are portrayed in the media, and we’ll consider how to rate the reliability of the various news sources available to us.  The specific topics have not be chosen in advance, but instead will be current events chosen in the course of the semester, based in part on students’ interests.
Finally, since this is a first year seminar, some class time will also be devoted to getting familiar with the resources available at Waseda University.
goal: In this class, students will build skills in reading, critical thinking, and discussion skills through a close reading or viewing of news articles and videos on a variety of topics. Writing skills will be strengthened through assignments in which students respond to the ideas raised in the readings and class discussions. Finally, students will develop creativity and planning skills in choosing topics and leading the class discussion for one class session.
study_outside:
Students should expect to spend two or more hours most weeks preparing for class. Before most classes, assigned to read three to four news articles on the topic for the week and sometimes to watch a short video. After some classes, they will be asked to write short reflection papers in response to the readings and class discussion.
For one week in the semester, students will work with a partner or small group to plan a class session: they will choose the readings, prepare discussion questions and a short presentation, and then lead the class discussion. Preparation for this will be done mainly outside of class time.
schedule_plan:
Provisional schedule: Note that the number of student-led sessions may be changed depending on the number of students enrolled in the class.
Weeks 1 to 9 will be led by the teacher, while later weeks will be led by groups of students.
Week 1: Introduction - Thinking about news sources and current issues of interest
Week 2: Focus on international issues, session 1
Week 3: Evaluating news sources
Week 4: Focus on international issues, session 2
Week 5: Focus on domestic (Japan) issues, session 1
Week 6: Focus on domestic (Japan) issues, session 2
Week 7: Focus on local (Tokyo) issues
Week 8: Mid-semester reflection, and planning for the second part of the semester
Week 9: Reading and discussion of a topic chosen by the teacher, to be announced
Week 10: Reading and discussion of a topic chosen by Group 1
Week 11: Reading and discussion of a topic chosen by Group 2
Week 12: Reading and discussion of a topic chosen by Group 3
Week 13: Reading and discussion of a topic chosen by Group 4
Week 14: Reading and discussion of a topic chosen by Group 5
textbook: There is no textbook for this class. Instead, materials will be read online or distributed in class.

summary_excerpt: After examining various competing theories of ethnic identity, national id......
subtitle: Social Identity: From Individual to Community
summary: After examining various competing theories of ethnic identity, national identity and nationalism, the last 6 weeks of the semester are set aside for discussion, preparation and delivery of student presentations. These presentations of approximately 15-minutes duration may be done in teams of two or three students, or as an individual project. Students will be required to make a presentation on the contemporary symbols and meaning of national identity in a location of their own choosing, and to analyze the evolution of that identity in terms of the ideas we discuss during the course.
goal: This course is designed to be part II of a two-part course in conjunction with my first semester IIB seminar. Students may choose to take just one or both of the courses. The second semester will focus on issues associated with group identities, such as ethnicity and national identity.
study_outside: As part of your preparation, you will be asked to read the materials posted on Waseda Moodle. Preparation is expected to take 90-120 minutes. For the review, you will be asked to submit an assignment, watch the on-demand content, or read the referential materials. The review is expected to take 90-120 minutes.
schedule_plan:
Weeks 1-2: We will begin with a review of concepts of identity and how they are rooted in the individual.
Weeks 3-5: Concepts of ethnicity will be examined in the work of Fredrik Barth and T.H. Eriksen.
Weeks 6-9: Two opposing models of the relationship between the development of the nation-state, nationalism and national identity will be examined in detail from the work of Eric J. Hobsbawm, Ernest Gellner, Benedict Anderson and Anthony D. Smith. A case study of national identity in contemporary Japan will sever as an example for students before they select their own cases for presentation.
Weeks 10-14: Discussion, preparation and delivery of student presentations.
The weekly schedule above is meant as a guide to the topics I hope to discuss in the semester. The order in which topics are presented may not follow this schedule precisely.
textbook: No specific text is assigned, but extensive reading will be required.
reference: A list of works, including those by the writers mentioned above, will be provided. Some copies will be distributed. A large amount of individual reading will be expected.
grading_method: Students will be required to make a presentation on the contemporary nature of national identity in a location of their own choosing, and to analyze the evolution of that identity in terms of the ideas we discuss during the course. The presentation should be approximately 15 minutes in length and show evidence of adequate research. A typed version should be handed to me in the final class, be properly annotated and contain a bibliography. The presentation will be marked out of 100. Any suspicion of plagiarism will result in the students concerned failing the course. In order to qualify for credits, students must attend at least 2/3 of all classes.

summary: This seminar is designed to enhance students’ academic skills through studying the history of the city and the area around the university through finding traces of the past on and around the Waseda campus. Students will first read various types of texts together to get background knowledge while improving their skills in critical reading. Then they will explore the campus and its surroundings to check what they have learned from the readings and find research questions. Finally, they will work on a research project, in which they will write an essay and make a presentation based on the essay.
goal:
1. Students can approach assignments in future courses and the senior thesis with confidence, integrity, and steady effort.
2. Students can exercise intellectual curiosity and formulate appropriate research topics for these assignments.
3. When working on these assignments, students can use the university library and academic resources effectively.
4. When working on these assignments, students can use AI appropriately.
5. Students can write coherent academic papers that present an argument rather than merely personal impressions, while avoiding plagiarism.
6. Students can give clear and persuasive presentations with confidence in front of others.
7. Students can collaborate effectively and contribute in a balanced way to group activities.
study_outside:
In the first sessions, students will read the assigned readings. There will be assignments to guide their reading.
Later, students will find materials for their presentations and essay. They will read the materials and put information together in the form of presentation and essay.
Additional activities will be necessary for group collaboration.
These altogether are expected to take 120-240 minutes every week.

name: An Introduction to Direct Democracy　51
summary_excerpt: This course deals with the history, theory and practice of direct democrac......
subtitle: History, Theory and Practice
summary:
This course deals with the history, theory and practice of direct democracy. Our historical journey starts from the ancient Greece and the Roman Republic－a time when direct democracy was originated, to the birth of contemporary direct democracy during the French revolution and in early modern Switzerland and New England, and further to the modern practice of direct democracy in the European Union.
In the light of the theories of direct democracy, we will then discuss the naive faith in, the hasty criticism against, and the widespread abuse of direct democracy. The course will be concluded in an open-ended debate on the role of direct democracy in the cosmopolitan world.
The course is organized mainly in the form of student-oriented introductory lecture. We will discuss introductory texts on direct democracy, and actually practice direct democracy in class!
As each course attendant will realize at the end of the course, active participation is not only the key to the success of direct democracy, but also the way to improve his/her own performance in this course. In addition to in-class discussion, each student will be required to write a short essay on direct democracy towards the end of the term.
goal: This course aims to decode the myth surrounding direct democracy. It helps students to better understand direct democracy as a contemporary　form of political participation.
study_outside: Basic knowledge of world history and politics is recommended.

[Class 12] Understanding Voting Behavior in Direct Democracy
[Class 13] Political Representation and Direct Democracy
[Class 14] Conclusion & Term Essay

summary_excerpt: In this class students will learn about the political system and political......
summary: In this class students will learn about the political system and political cultures of Germany, Switzerland and Austria (as well as the former GDR as a contrasting example). We will get to know political parties, civil society actors, and learn about protest dynamics and different participation forms within these liberal democratic systems as well as the role of labor unions and the other “social partners”. The class will assess the challenges of populism and growing authoritarianism on democratic discourse, and the role of the media systems in political deliberation. Different approaches to direct democracy will be thematized from a comparative point of view. The political system of the former GDR will serve as a historical example of a one-party-state without separation of powers.
goal: The objective of this class is to give students and overview of the core political institutions and electoral systems and political cultures of the German speaking countries (Germany, Austria, Switzerland) as well as a historical note on the former GDR.

summary:
※Online(On-Demand Recorded Video with Schedule Restriction)
In this course, we will study how students of politics have discussed political regimes and how their ideas have shaped our understanding of and actions in politics.
We will proceed by exploring representative classifications of political regimes, from the classical one developed by ancient Greeks, which defined democracy, oligarchy, aristocracy, tyranny, etc., to the modern one, which distinguished totalitarianism and authoritarianism, reflecting our contemporary experiences.
It is significant to know how these classifications divide regimes and what nature is attributed to each type of regime thus identified. For example, discussions on democracy have accumulated over many generations since antiquity. The nature and problems of democracy and the path a democracy tends to follow have already been studied well. This course will provide an introduction to this accumulated knowledge. Or modern times saw significant development in the typology of dictatorship. Totalitarianism and authoritarianism were newly recognized, followed by many sub-types of authoritarianism. This course will provide an overview of various contemporary political regimes, including these.
It is essential to study political regimes because the political regime we live under affects our lives inevitably. Furthermore, as antagonism between different political regimes has become a pivotal issue in world politics today, studying political regimes is even more significant.

In this course, we will study and think about “election”, the procedure by which we choose our representatives in the government. Elections are, in fact, the most significant element of the modern democratic political system. They are also the most visible and familiar part of the political process for ordinary citizens. Studying elections, therefore, serves as an excellent introduction to contemporary democracy as well as the political process at large.
During the semester, we will deal with the following topics:
The meaning and functions of elections.
The relationships between elections and democracies.
Elections under non-democratic regimes.
Several distinct types of electoral politics, such as clientelism and populism.
The variety of electoral systems and how to classify electoral systems.
The impact of electoral systems on the shape of politics.
Electoral strategies of political parties and candidates.
Various practices in electoral campaigning.
Politics of electoral reform, and so on.
Towards the end of the course, we will have sessions for case studies of the latest national elections in selected democracies. We will have Zoom meetings where students present their case studies on the assigned countries in groups. The meetings will take place on Thursday, 3rd Period in Weeks 11~13. All students will be required to attend the meetings.

name: APM- Anthropology of Labor: Key Issues and Cases　51
summary_excerpt: Labor is not only a classic theme in social science, but also a vital lens......
summary:
Labor is not only a classic theme in social science, but also a vital lens for understanding social development over the past century. This course introduces an anthropological way of understanding labor by focusing on how different forms of labor are made possible, organized, and evaluated under specific material and technological conditions. Rather than treating labor as an abstract or universal activity, the course examines labor as situated practice: shaped by tools, infrastructures, spatial arrangements, temporal regimes, and institutional frameworks.Through theoretical readings and ethnographic case studies, students will learn to analyze how concrete conditions give rise to particular forms of social relations, power asymmetries, moral expectations, and modes of subjectivity.
This course will tell the stories of different laborers,aiming not only to lead students to master multiple situations of labor (especially in the Chinese context), but also encourage a reflexive exploration of students finding their own positions in society and life.
goal: To strengthen the understanding of the ‘labor’ concept and living conditions of laborers in the Chinese context and the transition of Chinese society;
study_outside:
1.Everyone should spend some time reading relevant books or papers.The book list will be announced in the first class.
2.This course welcomes students from different cultures, teachers will assign corresponding reading tasks for students with diverse linguistic backgrounds. Unless under exceptional circumstances,
students are expected to conduct their classroom presentations and homework in English primarily. The teacher's lecture will use language consistent with reading literature and partly use Chinese to
elucidate cultural phenomena within specific contexts.
Preview and Review may take around 90-120 min. each.
schedule_plan:
The course is organized around the following 8 thematic units.
The specific pace and sequencing of the course may be adjusted according to classroom dynamics and learning progress.
1. Agricultural Labor: The Cultivator of the World
This unit examines agricultural labor as a foundational form of work shaped by land, tools, ecological conditions, and seasonal rhythms, and explores how these material conditions structure social cooperation and moral understandings of labor.
2. Skilled Labor
This unit focuses on skilled labor and craftsmanship, analyzing how expertise is produced, embodied, transmitted, and socially recognized through training, apprenticeship, and everyday practice.
3. Factory Labor
This unit explores factory labor in industrial and post-industrial settings, with attention to how machines, spatial organization, and temporal discipline reorganize labor processes and workers’ experiences.
4. Bureaucratic Labor
This unit examines labor within bureaucratic systems, focusing on how documents, procedures, and organizational hierarchies shape responsibility, authority, and everyday decision-making.
5. Labor: Globalization and Localization
This unit investigates labor under globalized conditions, analyzing how transnational standards, supply chains, and regulations interact with local practices and produce uneven outcomes.
6. Labor: Artificial Intelligence and the Platform Economy
This unit examines emerging forms of labor mediated by digital platforms and artificial intelligence, focusing on algorithmic management, data infrastructures, and new forms of labor control.
7. Labor: Service and Affective Work
This unit focuses on service and affective labor, analyzing how emotions, interpersonal interactions, and attitudes are organized, evaluated, and commodified within labor processes.
8. Labor: Gender and Family
This unit examines labor from the perspectives of gender and family, with particular attention to domestic work, care labor, and the organization of social reproduction.

summary_excerpt: A significant phenomenon in U.S. law, society and politics is the active r......
subtitle: Navigating the social and political divides
summary:
A significant phenomenon in U.S. law, society and politics is the active role of courts over many issues that divide the country, and the attention paid to judges,
especially U.S. Supreme Court justices, who differ in their orientations and can sway the outcome of issues that come to the Court.
This course will look into such important roles that the judicial branch in the U.S. and its judges have played in the evolution of the U.S. Constitution.
We will first look into theoretical considerations behind the role of the judiciary. Then we will look at how the U.S courts have performed this role, organized around three major themes: 1) the extent to which the ideology of the judges affect their decision-making; 2) the effectiveness of courts in bringing about social change; and 3) the tensions between the judiciary and the political branches.
We will examine the above items through cases that have divided U.S. society and politics-- such as abortion rights, same-sex marriage, gun regulation, racial and gender equality, and the President's power over immigration.

The method of course delivery will be Face-to-Face (F2F) (*Please note that if a sufficient number of students are unable to attend in-person because of travel restrictions, it may be necessary to move to Live Stream via Zoom).
This course is an advanced class, aimed at senior students, and offers what might be called an ‘advanced introduction’ to the European Union (EU), including its history, institutions, decision-making processes and policies.
An honest appraisal of the strengths and weaknesses of the EU is offered. The EU has been referred to as the most successful peace experiment in history, and the most successful international organization in history. The bases for both of these claims are examined. However the EU is also experiencing several interlocking and enduring crises, which some claim are a threat to the very future of the organization. These crisis include; the migration crisis, the Ukraine crisis, a ‘democratic deficit’, and Brexit. Each of these crises will be considered in some detail.
We also consider some of the key aspects of the EU’s international relations, with a focus on the role of the EU in the Asia-Pacific. We will study the EU’s relations with key state actors such as Japan, China, Russia, South Korea, Thailand and Vietnam, and also analyse how the EU has tried to promote several human rights norms in the region, using a variety of norm diffusion methods. We will also look at the EU’s attempts to engage with other governance projects in the region, including ASEAN, the Chinese Belt and Road Initiative, and the Free and Open Indo-Pacific promoted by the US, India and Australia, as well as Japan.

In this course, we will study political parties and party systems.
Political parties
are a fundamental element of modern political systems. We will examine their role in different political regimes and highlight their indispensability to modern democracies. We will also look back in history to understand how political parties, by nature mere voluntary associations, became essential instruments of contemporary politics. We will see how different types of political parties have emerged one after another in response to societal changes. Eventually, we will take up a classification scheme meant to encompass all existing political parties and obtain the basis for discussing any political party.
A party system
arises from and shapes the competition among political parties for elected office. Thus, the form of a party system depends on the rules of electoral competition but also interacts with the electoral strategies and performance of political parties. It also reflects the nature of the broader political system. For example, a one-party system indicates a particular type of dictatorship, while a competitive party system is a hallmark of democracy. In addition, two-party and multi-party systems represent different models of democracy. Moreover, a party system reflects the state of political society, mirroring social divisions while reinforcing, mitigating, or even creating them. We will explore these multiple aspects of a party system.
Political parties and party systems are not products of legislation: parties are inherently voluntary associations
and
party systems are largely spontaneous orders, even though both often look like formal state institutions. As such, they are difficult to pin down. However, there is a wealth of studies - observations, typologies, and theories - that can help us approach these phenomena. In this course, we will draw on the works of prominent scholars in the field to grasp the essentials of political parties and party systems.

It encourages a critical examination of competing conceptions of democracy and their relevance for addressing new political challenges.

name: Introduction to History　51
summary_excerpt: Recent scholarship offers a perspective that diverges significantly from t......
summary:
Recent scholarship offers a perspective that diverges significantly from traditional history textbooks. The field has expanded and diversified, increasingly adopting interdisciplinary methods. This course serves as an introduction to the current state of historical studies. While students may be accustomed to a passive learning environment, they will be expected to approach history as an active subject of critical inquiry.
The class is structured around three core components:
Historiography and Theory: We will examine how history is written and how our understanding of the past has evolved.
Methodology and Practice: By analyzing a wide range of materials—from government records to films and popular music—lectures will demonstrate the primary methods used to practice history.
Conceptual Frameworks: Key historical concepts, such as colonialism, memory, and nationalism, will be reinterpreted through the lens of other scholarly disciplines. Through these discussions, we will trace the shifting landscape of modern historical studies.
