name: History and Narrative in Premodern Japan 51
summary_excerpt: This course explores various aspects of classical and early medieval Japan......
subtitle: From Nara and Heian to Kamakura
summary:
This course explores various aspects of classical and early medieval Japan (circa 8th to 13th centuries) by listening to different voices recorded in historical and literary sources. The sessions will alternate in focus: first they will take up the history of a particular time or topic and then they will explore a related literary works. The course aims to expand our perspective and reshape our understanding of Japanese history as a complex and nonlinear process.
In addition to the lectures, the class will emphasize discussions based on a critical analysis of reading materials, including diverse literary texts in English translation. Students will be required to read, think, and share their views regularly throughout the semester.
As the participants usually comprise both local and international students with diverse regional and educational backgrounds, the course will be a good platform for you to meet new ideas and explore not only events in the past but also contemporary issues relevant to yourself. Students who just started to learn Japanese culture, including SP3/SP4 students, are by all means welcome, and no prior knowledge of Japanese history or literature is required to enroll. Please just note that you may (at least in the beginning) struggle with unfamiliar names, terms, and concepts, and will need to spend some extra time looking up those names and terms. Students who have previously studied Japanese history and classical literature are certainly also welcome. Those of you will be required to revisit your knowledge, especially if you have only studied the subject at Japanese elementary and/or secondary schools, and devise how to present your ideas in an academic fashion that makes sense in an international context.

This course serves as an introduction to the fundamental issues of modern Japanese history, emphasizing the interplay between international and domestic factors in Japan’s development. The lectures cover the period from the 1840s to the present.

subtitle: Modern British History, 1688-Present
summary:
Modern British History
This course will be a survey of the history of Great Britain from the Revolution of 1688 to Brexit. Its main purpose is to help you understand from a historical perspective how Britain and the British came to be the way they are at present, including economy, society, politics, and culture. Britain today is a multi-national state that once included, though it does not now, all of the peoples of the British Isles. Therefore, the course will deal with the Scots, Irish, and Welsh, as well as the English. The main theme of the course will be the rise and fall of British power and influence: the expansion of English power within the British Isles, the formation of the United Kingdom of Great Britain, the transformation of a traditional society, the rise and decline of British industrial power, the development of a class society, and the rise and fall of Britain as a great power. Britain was the world’s first “modern” nation, and in the nineteenth century Britain was the greatest power on earth. But Britain now has receded from great power status, and the British (especially the English) are uncertain about their global role and even their national identity. In each development Britain has been (and is) an object lesson for other countries such as Japan and the United States.

summary:
This course focuses on how ancient Rome was used and revived in the history of Italy. The Colosseum (originally named the Flavian Amphitheater) was inaugurated in 80 CE, and from this time on, this huge monument stands in the city of Rome and has captured the attention of residents and travelers alike due to its scale. Various individuals have left impressions and opinions about the Colosseum through books, letters, and diaries, allowing us to trace the transformation of its image over time.
To analyze this issue, firstly, we will explore the role and function of the Colosseum in Ancient Rome. This analysis will enable us to deepen our understanding of ancient society. Subsequently, we will examine the diverse images the Colosseum assumed in later periods. In some instances, the Colosseum presents unexpected faces, closely linked to historical assumptions about ancient Rome in each era. Through this process, we will analyze the transformation of the memory of the Colosseum, seeking to understand how Italian society used ancient Rome to solve its problems. This examination prompts us to consider how our current image of the past has evolved.

summary_excerpt: Given the fact that nobody seems able to avoid the influence of the Unite......
subtitle: Division and Diversity
summary:
Given the fact that nobody seems able to avoid the influence of the United States, whether you like it or not, it is beneficial to understand how and why the world's first democratic nation has become such a dominant powerhouse in a short period of time.
This course examines some of the historical topics pertinent to the current United States, such as slavery (racism and wealth gap), the Civil War (political division, unified nation-statehood), Reconstruction (definition of American citizenship and equal protection of the law), and Jim Crow (inequality). The subject of slavery reminds us that the United States was established as a slaveholding nation, while it would not have become a consolidated capitalist nation without the abolition of slavery through the Civil War. Constitutional amendments enacted during Reconstruction, such as the 14th and 15th amendments laid the foundation for equality among people of color, women, and immigrants. And it was during the Jim Crow era when discrimination against non-white people, including Asians, gained legitimacy. As some scholars argue, Jim Crow, rather than slavery, has the lasting impact on American society of today.
By focusing on those topics, students will have a better grasp of other members of the country, such as Native Americans, and ideas of democracy, conservatism, and liberalism.
goal: The goal of this course is to dispel widely-held but false ideas about some of the current issues by situating the selected topics within the history of the United States and that of the world as a whole.

name: Seminar on History  53
teacher: ステレンバーグ　マシュー　ケイン
summary_excerpt: This advanced seminar is for students who have a keen interest in history,......
subtitle: Theories and Methods in History
summary:
This advanced seminar is for students who have a keen interest in history, want to sharpen their ability to think historically, and intend to write a graduation thesis on an historical topic. The seminar has three main goals: 1) to equip students with a a deeper understanding of the theories and methods (also known as historiography) that underlie historical research, 2) to help students develop a deeper appreciation of what historical research can “do,” that is, the kinds of questions it can answer and the sort of insights it can offer; and 3) to help students choose a viable thesis topic, conduct substantial research on it, and shape that research into a persuasive graduation thesis. How we accomplish these goals will vary from semester to semester depending on enrollment and student interests, but the essential format of the seminar is discussion of assigned readings. What will we read? Typically, we will begin the semester by reading essays and excerpts that relate to Goal #1 above. These readings address questions such as: what is history? how do historians evaluate evidence? what counts as a good historical explanation of an event? Is there such a thing as historical truth?
After a few weeks of this we will usually transition to considering Goal #2 above, and this means reading an exemplary historical monograph. Based on the instructor’s suggestions, together we will choose a book that addresses an important and relevant topic, that is interesting and well-written, and that reveals what historical research can do in the hands of a master practitioner. (Usually these books are in the field of modern British, European, or transatlantic history. Recent choices have included Hyperactive: The Controversial History of ADHD by Matthew Smith, Return from the Natives: How Margaret Mead Won the Second World War and Lost the Cold War by Peter Mandler, and Family Secrets: Shame and Privacy in Modern Britain by Deborah Cohen.)
Parallel to all of this we will be addressing Goal #3, which means that we will have regular consultations about how to choose and research a thesis topic, how your research is progressing, and how to transform that research into a finished thesis.
Believe it or not, while learning all of this we can and will have some fun along the way. We’ll be reading fascinating documents and thinking about important questions. Consequently, this course will include an ample amount of debate and discussion. I want to hear what you think and how you think about the issues we cover.
goal: By the end of this seminar students will have substantial knowledge of the issues and debates that have shaped, and continue to shape, the historical profession. In addition they will have improved their ability to think historically and developed skills in historical research and writing that will allow them to pursue graduate study in history if they so choose.

The seminar sessions will have two main components: 1) discussions based on assigned readings (and ideally field trips) and 2) a workshop for writing the thesis.

While acknowledging the significance that the modern discipline of history has attached to facts and the process of substantiating them, we will experience together the pains and problems of writing histories and sharing memories.

summary:
The system of this lecture is F2F.
The principal aim of this course is to provide for the students an introduction of African studies, especially in Southern African Countries. While the African continent has significant legal, political and economic challenges, students are rarely introduced to the attempts of African states to set up structures to confront those challenges through regional integration. This course will introduce students to the various legal, political and economic regional integration initiatives in the Southern African region which has become an emerging region.
Under the powerful influence of South Africa’s significantly accelerating growth, the economic fortunes of Southern Africa as a whole should experience a major boost from 2010. With the region’s dominant economic power finally shaking off some of the heavy burdens of its inherited domestic problems and beginning to forge ahead much more convincingly, most countries in its closest orbit can expect to see positive gains in terms of improved trade and investment flows.
However, because Southern Africa is yet some way from being a truly cohesive economic bloc, a few contradictory and negative influences are still at work. These are seen most notably in Zimbabwe’s long-running political and economic meltdown; in Angola’s poor economic management in the midst of its latest oil revenue windfall; and in the persistence of drought and rural distress in Malawi. Most importantly, the overall trends are positive, and at least nine countries have been notching up growth rates in excess of 6％ a year. These include the familiar strong performers, like Botswana and Mauritius, as well as the best practitioners of fundamental economic reform like Mozambique and Zambia. The highest growth rate, Mozambique’s 7％ in 2020, may seem to be in a league of its own but in reality, reflected no more than the buoyancy of the natural gas sector.
From the copper of Zambia to Angola’s oil and Namibia’s uranium, many counties in the region are dependent on the export of unprocessed commodities. Looking for lessons on what works? Botswana and South Africa have been successful in attracting value-added processing.
The Tripartite Free Trade Area(TFTA) is a new continental integration project between the SADC, COMESA, and the EAC, expected to be operational by 2021 or 2022.
Now the COVID-19 affects the region, especially South Africa. As of August 2021, South Africa has the highest number of COVID-19 cases in Africa, but with a relatively low death rate.
In that connection, students will learn a lot about the region. This unique lecture at Waseda University started in 2008. In this lecture, each Ambassadors and Embassy officials from the SADC (Southern African Development Community) (http://www.sadc.int/) group will make a presentation on the variety of SADC regions, in terms of the Economy and Politics and the relationship between Japan and the SADC region during this class. In Japan, there are actually 12 embassies of SADC (Angola, Botswana, Democratic Republic of Congo, Lesotho, Madagascar, Malawi, Mozambique, Namibia, South Africa, Tanzania, Zambia, and Zimbabwe) (For a moment Mauritius, Seychelles, Eswatini(Former Swaziland) and Comores do not have Embassy in Japan). This SADC group is the biggest diplomatic group among the African Diplomatic Corps in Tokyo. The course will focus on the geopolitical area of southern Africa, and the issues that such regions face as they plan to seek to integrate their local economies.

subtitle: Transoceanian Studies 1
summary:
Iakwe! Kaselehlie mai! Hafa Adai! Alii! Aloha! Aroha! Ia Ora Na! Kia Orana! Welcome to Oceania!
When people in Japan talk about the Pacific Ocean, usually they think about a big, vast sea, with America on the other side. They think of tropical islands and hula dancing, or mysterious military operations, tuna fish and other seafood. Usually we don’t consider that, from a Japanese perspective, the Pacific is what connects us to the United States and the rest of the world. We forget about the Pacific War or about the other ways that the Pacific links Japan to the United States, and instead we just talk about ideas like “the American dream,”“freedom,” fast food, or economic power. Some people have referred to the Pacific Ocean as “an American Lake,” when referring to American military and economic power. In this class, will take this into consideration and take a very different approach to “America," "Japan," and "gender relations" through "international relations," by thinking of how these things are seen from the vast communities of people who live on islands in the Pacific Ocean. .” The great Tongan scholar Epeli Hau’ofa called the Pacific Ocean a “Sea of Islands.” By this, he meant that usually we think of the Pacific as a big, empty ocean, but in fact it is filled with thousands of islands that are all connected to each other and that all connect everyone in the world together. His message was that we should take Oceania seriously and realize our deep ties to this place and to each other. Especially during the times of this new coronavirus pandemic, and amidst the tides of massive climate change that deeply affects the Pacific Islands, this course takes on more urgency and relevance for all of us.
First and foremost, this is a course about appreciating and empathizing with historical narratives on many levels, exploring histories of empire, war, and globalization from the perspectives of indigenous Pacific Islanders. Although this history is not well known by neither Japanese nor Americans, the Pacific history of the islands between these two countries is very important for understanding the history of the 20th century. This will be a very unique opportunity to get a new awareness not only of America but of militarization, nuclear weapons, globalization, climate change, international politics, and historical popular culture--and especially Japan--through the eyes of the Pacific Islanders who have the closest connections to Japan and the United States. Moreover, we take a deeper reading on how gender plays a big part in colonialism, militarization, and power/ How have Pacific Islanders been influenced by Japan and America? How have we in continental nations been influenced by Pacific Islanders? How did World WarⅡconnect and divide Japan and America? What remains of the war in the Pacific, and what is remembered or forgotten? How does this play into nationalism today? Using the metaphor of “coral” and the “reef,” we will talk about how each and every one of us is somehow related to the Pacific Islands, and we will look closely at the Pacific to give us many serious examples about major issues that affect the whole world. Many people say that the Pacific is the most globalized--and also the most American place on earth. Let’s explore why.
goal: This is a large lecture class, taught in person. By the end of this class, you will be expected to have a basic historical understanding of early settlement, navigation, European and Japanese colonialism, and war in Oceania from the perspectives of Pacific Islands, with a particular emphasis on how America and Japan are connected through Oceania. You will be challenged to rethink your assumptions about America and Japan, and to try to creatively think of new ways of approaching globalization and change so that Islander and other indigenous or marginalized perspectives are also taken into consideration. Hopefully you will also have a better understanding of our shared histories and have a better idea of how we can all cooperate to create a better world.

summary:
The system of this lecture is F2F.
Africa is often perceived by the average Japanese as a continent of conflict and contagion, as the “dark continent,” chaotic and mysterious, or as a continent with wild animals and plants living throughout. In other words, Africa is a continent very far from Japan and Asia, both geographically and psychologically. Hopefully, through this course, students will find a different, more complex reality, a reality where people and countries, like the rest of the world, are struggling with war and peace, authoritarianism and democracy, colonial legacies and current dilemmas, and a reality that calls into question some of the most fundamental beliefs and theories about international relations.
In that connection, this course will try to provide an overview of the politics of sub-Saharan Africa and will examine the social, political, and economic systems in several countries in sub-Saharan Africa. We will also examine major problems facing African states and their citizens. The lectures and discussions will focus on the historical and social legacies that have shaped modern sub-Saharan Africa, and the current social, political, and economic circumstances in that region. We will explore early post-independence Africa, the liberation movements, the authoritarian regimes of the late 1960s to the early 1980s, and some important current social, political, and economic issues. We will examine how the governments and people in sub-Saharan Africa have responded to these issues and attempt to offer possible routes to a brighter political and economic future. We will try to understand the specificities of the current conflicts in Africa and we will consider how to bring these conflicts to an end and prevent their recurrence.
Now the COVID-19 affects the region, especially South Africa. As of August 2021, South Africa has the highest number of COVID-19 cases in Africa, but with a relatively low death rate. COVID-19 death rates have been low and the share of recoveries high in Africa despite earlier warnings from experts that the virus would overrun weak health systems in most countries and kill millions. However, Africa is still needing assistance to bear on the COVID-19 pandemic. Africa is still needing the COVID-19 vaccines also. The rate of vaccination in the whole of Africa is less than 1% as of August 2021. The principal aim of this course is to introduce students to the study of contemporary sub-Saharan African politics and issues. It will expose students to the great diversity of peoples, ideas, cultures, and economic and political systems in this region of the world. In addition, the course will familiarize students with the contemporary social, political, and economic issues being debated by analysts of sub-Saharan African politics. The course will help students develop a broader knowledge of how politics affect the millions of people living in the region. The Instructor will organize a special lecture with African Diplomatic Corps (ADC) in Tokyo within this lecture with the realm of possibility. Lastly, Japan is organizing its important policy forum on Africa, TICAD (Tokyo International Conference on African Development) since 1993. TICAD Ⅵ was held in Nairobi in 2016. TICAD 7 was held in Japan in 2019. TICAD 8 was held in Africa (Tunisia) in 2022. The instructor will explain the role of Japan in African development. TICAD 9 wiil be held in Yokohama in 2025.

name: History and Philosophy of Science
teacher: シドリ　ネイサン　カミッロ
summary_excerpt: Science and technology have become defining features of modern life. In th......
summary:
Science and technology have become defining features of modern life. In this course, we will explore aspects of the history of human thought about the natural world and philosophical ideas about the special status of scientific knowledge by focusing attention on three episodes in the history of science - the development of rational, mathematical accounts of the world in the ancient and medieval periods, the transformation of this in the early modern period that resulted in the Newtonian worldview and, finally, the development of the new physics of the early 20th century.
We will examine these topics in the history of science using themes in contemporary philosophy of science. While the topics of the lectures are structured around episodes and figures in the history of science, each class we will also reflect on how the history of science has been used by philosophers of science to provided examples for the key themes in the philosophy of science, such as the relationship between theory and evidence, the verifiability or falsifiability of theories and the historical contingency of scientific practice. Students who apply themselves in this class will learn the broad chronological development of the physical sciences, how to appreciate science as a social institution, and obtain insight into major shifts in overall worldview that have taken place in conjunction with the growth of the sciences.

summary: Traditional biology is the study of the rules of morphology, classification, evolution, behavior, and genetics of living organisms. The fields of medicine, pharmacology, agriculture, and chemistry have included biochemistry, which studies the structure and function of molecules comprising living organisms from the perspective of chemistry. Biochemistry and molecular biology are closely associated with each other, and together they continue to provide important insights for the development of the biotechnologies. The achievements of this research form the basis for various applied technologies in the fields of medicine, pharmacology, and agriculture.
goal: This lecture covers the molecules that constitute living organisms and their control mechanisms, as well as biotechnologies and the principles of aging and disease. Students are expected to acquire the abilities to understand and explore biological system at the molecular and cellular level.

name: Environmental Pollution and Control 51
summary_excerpt: This course is designed to learn the cause and mechanisms of environmental......
subtitle: Environmental Pollution
summary: This course is designed to learn the cause and mechanisms of environmental pollution that human beings have experienced and are still going on today. First, we focus on environmental laws, regulations and international agreements to prevent further destruction of the Earth's environment. Secondly, we learn about chemical pollution and its effect on ecosystems and on human beings. Areas include greenhouse gas emission and acid rain from fossil fuel combustion, synthetic chemical usage in intensive agriculture causing bioaccumulation and eutrophication, cyanobacterial bloom and intoxication of drinking water, and DNA pollution examples in horticulture and in fisheries will also be discussed. Thirdly, we go through the pollution control measures, focusing on waste water treatment, groundwater protection, and bioremediation technologies, and look at some measurement and modelling examples developed under environmental regulations and the Environmental Impact Assessment Law. Lastly, we find the solution to prevent further pollution, by applying alternative energy sources/renewable energy usage, and notice the importance of watershed basin/ catchment-level point of view to manage and solve complex problems. This course consists of lectures, discussions and assignments.　※The class will be taught by On-Demand format, but each class's video is available until the next week.
goal: To understand the cause of environmental pollution, and be able to explain our present situation and how human activities degrade our environment. Become aware of the prevention measures and acquire watershed/basin point of view to solve such complex environmental problems.
study_outside:
Study about the Muskie Law, Kyoto Protocol and Paris Agreement. It takes about 2 hours in total, but could be any time before attending each class.
Survey where your waste water goes. This assignment will be given anytime within the course.
schedule_plan:
1:
Vol. 1 Introduction to the course
Course description, requirements and the topics on law regulations, international agreements and protocols on environmental pollution control will be explained.
2:
Vol. 2 Cause and effect of air pollution
Air pollutants from combustion of fossil fuels in our industrial society will be described. The mechanism and impact of acid rain and its control will be discussed.
3:
Vol. 3 Water pollution from industries and agriculture
We will discuss not only on toxic chemicals from industries, but also on excess nutrient and soluble substance input from agricultural field, golf courses, and our daily water usages that cause eutrophication and degradation of freshwater quality.
4:
Vol. 4 Mechanism of bioaccumulation
Learn about the accumulation of toxic chemicals, heavy metals and radioactive substances into organisms through food-web and biotic interactions. Lead, PCB, mercury, and cadmium poisoning examples will be discussed.
5:
Vol. 5 Problem of cyanobacterial bloom and its control measures
The blue-green algal bloom in freshwater produces carcinogen that is harmful to human beings. Some monitoring results from the Great Lakes region and the Lake Kasumigaura will be discussed.
6:
Vol. 6 Waste water treatment system
Learn about the technologies used in sewage water treatment, removal of heavy metals, and re-use of nutrient-rich water for pilot farms as bioremediation in Michigan.
7:
Vol. 7 Groundwater pollution
We will learn about the cause of groundwater pollution from landfills of toxic waste, and discuss bewildering handling of nuclear wastes.
8:
Vol. 8 Oceanic pollution
We will learn about the fate of microplastics (micro-beads) accumulated in ocean and marine fauna. Also we discuss acidification of ocean water and coral bleaching problems.
9:
Vol. 9 Methods to detect and measure environmental pollutants
We learn about water testing methods and discuss on Microcystis (blue-green algae) bloom monitoring in the Great Lakes, and talk about the new environmental DNA method, which detects the presence of aquatic invasive species by sampling of water, in Japanese rivers.
10:
Vol.10 Pollen pollution as a result of mono-cultural plantation
Under-use of monoculture tree resources is causing pollen allergy and soil erosion problems in Japan. Also, from a disease control point of view, we will learn about some examples of pest and disease outbreaks related to intensive agriculture and deforestation.
11:
Vol.11 Genetic pollution risks from GMOs and introduced species.
Learn about the risk of genetically engineered or modified organism (GMO) usage in crop fields and DNA pollution in the surrounding environment. Also, the risk of using "Greening" plants and introduced pets from overseas will be discussed.
12:
Vol.12 DNA pollution from fish release practices
We will learn about the risk of transporting and releasing of fish hatched in different watersheds. Contamination and genetic identity loss of local populations caused by genetic introgression of "domestically" introduced species will be discussed.
13:
Vol.13 Sound, odor, vibration, electromagnetic wave and space debris pollutions
We now discuss on the new types of pollutants that we could control by providing adequate international laws, regulations,and Life-Cycle Assessment (LCA).
14:
Vol.14 Necessity of catchment /watershed point of view for problem-solving (Final)
Learn about the importance of describing environmental processes and pollution regime from catchment-basin (watershed) point of view (final lecture).

name: History of Mathematics　51
teacher: シドリ　ネイサン　カミッロ
summary_excerpt: For most of western history, an understanding of mathematical proof was co......
subtitle: History of Mathematics
summary:
For most of western history, an understanding of mathematical proof was considered essential to a well-rounded education. There is the common story that Abraham Lincoln always carried with him a copy of Euclid’s Elements. Cicero tells us that he sought out the grave of Archimedes, in order to pay tribute to one of the great icons of the intellectual culture he wished to emulate. Neither of these men had any advanced training in mathematics; they were statesmen and orators. They read mathematics because it can compel with a force far beyond that of great speeches. Mathematics is capable of convincing us of things we can all agree upon, and it does this through rigorous proof.
This course explores the origins of various types of deductive argumentation by working through the arguments of proofs in a historical context. We will look at the sources of different approaches to mathematical demonstrations in a number of diverse cultures and periods. We focus on the continuous tradition that began in Greece, was adopted by Arabic and Hebrew scholars, and was further cultivated in the Latin west. Finally, we will confront contemporary challenges to the idea of proof such as the delicate relationship between rigor and intelligibility and the possibility of computer generated proofs.
Although this is not a mathematics course, you should have some familiarity in mathematics and mathematical ideas. The texts will demand careful attention to the reasoning but they will not require advanced mathematical training. Although it is important to understand the mathematical arguments, we will also pay attention to the text’s historical and philosophical aspects. Each time we meet, we will work through a number of proofs on the board.
[Note: This course will be conducted face-to-face (フル対面). Students are not allowed to use
mobile phones
,

, or
laptops
in class.]

summary:
Thiscourse assumes a foundational understanding of probability and statistics. Wewill begin by reviewing these concepts using Excel, Python, and R, and thenexamine extensions of multivariate regression analysis

goal:
This course aims to develop foundational skills in the following areas:
1. Efficiently and appropriately organizing and analyzing data using Excel, Python, and R.
2. Quantitatively expressing dependencies within cross-sectional data and providing logical explanations or making judgments based on those findings.
3. Quantitatively measuring the magnitude of effects resulting from interventions, such as specific treatments or policies, using data.
4. Identifying temporal dependency structures in time-series data and generating future forecasts based on data available up to the present.

summary:
IMPORTANT: This course will be taught Face-To-Face.
This is an advanced-level course on Data Science. The course will focus on deep learning, which has witnessed great success over the past decade. Image processing and natural language processing are two of the most successful fields of deep learning. Some of the most successful applications of deep learning in image processing include object detection, image segmentation, and image classification. In natural language processing, deep learning has been used to develop applications such as machine translation, text classification, automatic summarization and question answering.
The course will begin with an overview of the PyTorch library, a standard  library used for deep learning. Students will then study linear algebra and calculus from numerical perspectives.  After a gentle introduction of neural network models using the familiar linear and softmax regression, the concept of multilayer perceptrons and the essential technique of backward propagation will be introduced. Various ways to regularize deep neural networks will be studied, such as putting norm penalties or allowing dropout, and students will learn how to do optimization for training these regularized deep neural networks.
In the latter portion of this course, the students will learn convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for image analysis and learn neural network models for natural language processing (NLP). The students will learn the state-of-the-art transformer models for NLP.  Students will learn how to use and fine-tune pretrained large language models including BERT, T5 and GPT models.
An integral component of this course is project-based learning, where students will engage in two major group projects. The first project will revolve around the application of multilayer perceptrons in tasks involving regression and classification. In the second project students will explore the use of modern deep neural network models in either image analysis or NLP challenges.

subtitle: Advanced Seminar on Data Science
summary:
IMPORTANT: This course will be taught Face-To-Face.
This seminar is designed for students who are interested in data science, a relatively new field of study that combines aspects of computer science and statistics to extract valuable insights from data. Data science is sometimes defined as the practice of collecting, cleaning, and analyzing data to draw conclusions and make decisions. Data science is important to all of us because it allows us to make better decisions by turning data into insights. Recent achievements of data science include the development of new ways to analyze social media data and predictive models that can be used for things like detecting credit card fraud or identifying cancerous tumors. Additionally, data science has been used to develop recommendation systems for book, movie and music streaming services.
In this seminar, we will take a practical approach to learning data science through extensive examples using the popular programming language Python. Students interested in both theory and applications in data science, with or without much previous exposure to Python, are welcomed to join this seminar. The first half of the seminar (Vol.1 to Vol. 6) focuses on learning Python. We will gently dive into data science by introducing Python and the convenient tool of Jupyter Notebook. Students with relatively lesser previous exposure to Python are expected to do more self-study on learning Python programming in order to catch up with others. Students will learn how to use the most important libraries, namely, NumPy and Pandas, the former being the basic for scientific computation and the latter for manipulation of data. Students will also learn basics of data visualization using the standard library Matplotlib. The second half of the seminar (Vol.7 to Vol. 14) focuses on learning of basic machine learning algorithms. Vol. 7 introduces the basic problems of machine learning and the basic library Scikit-Learn for implementing most of the machine learning algorithms to be learned later on. Students will learn basic concepts of a couple of core machine learning algorithms and how to implement them. These core algorithms include, but not limited to, naive Bayes for classification, linear regression for prediction, support vector machines for classification, decision trees for classification and prediction, principal component analysis for dimension reduction, k-means algorithm for clustering, and Gaussian mixture models for clustering and density estimation.
Students who possess a sufficient background in data science and proficiency in Python programming may directly commence their thesis research on topics within the field of data science.
goal: In this seminar, students will obtain basic knowledge in Python which will be sufficient for implementing most of the core machine learning algorithms. Students will also learn some selected machine learning algorithms that are important for a wide range of problems in industry and academia.

summary:
The method of course delivery will be Face-to-Face (F2F) (*Please note that if a sufficient number of students are unable to attend in-person because of travel restrictions, it may be necessary to move to Live Stream via Zoom).
In this class we study the theory and practice of humanitarian intervention. Is it ever justifiable to intervene in the domestic affairs of another sovereign state? If so, when, and for what reasons?
We consider the possibility that a norm of humanitarian intervention has emerged in international society since the end of the Cold War, by examining case studies of most of the major intervention cases that have arisen in the last twenty years. Case studies include Iraq 1991, Somalia, Rwanda, Bosnia, Kosovo, Afghanistan, Iraq 2003, Darfur, Libya, Syria.
goal: Students will acquire a comprehensive understanding of each of the specific cases listed above, and develop the capacity to evaluate the legality, legitimacy and effectiveness of humanitarian intervention. We will study the UN Charter in detail, and consider the extent to which the ‘responsibility to protect’, an influential concept that has been endorsed by the UN, can guide us in our future debates about when to intervene in other sovereign states for human protection purposes.

name: Introduction to Islamic Culture
summary_excerpt: Islam is currently the world's second-largest religion, following Christia......
summary:
Islam is currently the world's second-largest religion, following Christianity, with Muslims (adherents of Islam) comprising nearly one-fourth of the global population. Due to its faster growth rate compared to Christianity, Islam is expected to become the world's largest religion in the near future.
Although Islam originated in the seventh-century Arabian Peninsula, the majority of Muslims today live outside the Arab region. The Asia-Pacific region is home to the largest Muslim-majority countries, including Indonesia, Pakistan, and Bangladesh. Even in Japan, where Muslims are a minority, there are around 230,000 adherents, underscoring the importance of understanding Islam in the contemporary world.
The course will cover a broad range of topics, including the geographic distribution of Muslims, the diversity within Islam, the Abrahamic religions, pre-Islamic Arabia, the life of Prophet Muhammad and the origins of Islam, fundamental beliefs and practices, the Quran and Hadith, Islamic celebrations and daily life, Islamic law, religious scholars (ulama) and theological seminaries (madrasas), sectarian differences (Sunni and Shia), and Sufism (Islamic mysticism). While recognizing the rich diversity of Islamic practices, the course will focus on the core beliefs and obligatory practices universally accepted by Muslims across different regions. summary_excerpt: This course aims to deepen students' understanding of the Middle East by e......
subtitle: State and Society in the Middle East
summary:
This course aims to deepen students' understanding of the Middle East by exploring key concepts and theories that illuminate the formation of states, the unique features of political systems, and the socio-economic challenges faced by the region's inhabitants, particularly the youth, in contemporary times.
The course will cover topics such as state formation, colonialism, authoritarianism, rentier states, clientelism, monarchies, and republics, as well as the Arab uprisings, with the goal of understanding the characteristics of Middle Eastern states. To analyze the complex challenges confronting Middle Eastern societies, we will examine issues like demographic transition, the youth bulge, the expansion of higher education, academic credentialism, graduate unemployment, brain drain, waithood, gender and Islam, marriage and divorce, and the growing discontent among youth. Through the assigned readings, students will develop the skills necessary to analyze these issues from multiple perspectives, leading to a more nuanced and comprehensive understanding of the Middle East.
As this course will be conducted in person, regular attendance is mandatory for all students. Please note that there will be no online distribution or simultaneous virtual sessions available.
goal:
This course aims to achieve the following goals:
1. Develop an understanding of the historical origins and evolution of modern states in the Middle East.
2. Acquire useful conceptual frameworks for effectively assessing the characteristics of political regimes and comparing the governing systems of Middle Eastern countries.
3. Become familiar with concepts and theories relevant to analyzing the challenges and concerns faced by people in the region, particularly the younger generation, and apply these frameworks to the study of Middle Eastern societies.

**
Course Overview: Blaise Pascal's Pensées
**
The Pensées of Blaise Pascal (1623-1662), celebrated as both a scientific genius and a profound religious thinker, is widely regarded as a classic work of the French seventeenth Century. This period marked the dawn of Modernity, a time when people began to question the Dignity of humanity at the crossroads of Science and Religion, Order and Revolution, Greatness and Misery.
In this Course, students will develop a nuanced understanding of this philosophical text while deepening their knowledge of French Thought and Religion through the reading and analysis of Pascal's Pensées. The Course will also cover its Reception History, explore various themes related to Life, Humanity, and Religion, and encourage students to express their own existential reflections. Classes will be conducted in person during the first week (orientation) and the last week (in-class essay writing) (each time one period of 100 minutes). For the 3rd and 4th weeks (group discussions) and the 13th-14th weeks (presentations), classes will be held via real-time streaming. For the remaining weeks of the semester, students will engage with the texts and write comments and essays based on assigned video.
**This Course is designed to be on-demand, except for a few scheduled classes.

summary_excerpt: This course implements an integral reading of core classical philosophical......
summary: This course implements an integral reading of core classical philosophical texts in Ethics. The lecture covers one author and theme by the two classes. This semester, we will read two studies compiled in Emmanuel Levinas, Of God Who Comes to Mind. The class will focus on “Dialogue: Self-Consciousness and Proximity of the Neighbor”, and continue by reading“Notes On Meaning”.
goal: The objectives of this course is to strengthen student’s knowledge in sophisticated ethical theories. During the class, we will field questions such as: What is the difference between ethics and morality? In what sense ethical might be radical? What is the difference between ethics and philosophy?
study_outside:
Please read painstakingly in advance the chapters of the essays selected in Of God Who Comes To Mind, as indicated in the course schedule, including the endnotes.
Students are asked to search for the meaning of unfamiliar English terms (for example, “interestedness” p. 138). They also have to train themselves in identifying concepts that they potentially cannot define by themselves (for example, “immanence”, p. 137), and to search for their meaning in authoritative dictionaries and encyclopedia of philosophy (see the “References” section below).
Advices
1. Please train yourselves for the final exam in taking handwritten notes.
2. Don’t stay alone with Levinas! Work in group of 2 to 4! Play the game, behave such as a philosopher! 3. Resume each session, formulate questions to ask during the class and anticipate the possible questions that will be asked to you during the final exam.

summary_excerpt: This class explores the ethics of public office as a central political iss......
subtitle: A Comparison of French and American Political Ethics
summary: This class explores the ethics of public office as a central political issue sitting at the intersection of political theory, the history of political thought, democratic practice, and institutional design. The course provides an overview of contemporary debates in political ethics through a comparative analysis of French and American political traditions in order to trace the historical roots of their distinct political-ethical cultures and highlight contrasting conceptions of public responsibility, political representation and democratic legitimacy.
goal:
By the end of the course, students will:
- Understand major past and present theories of political ethics, as well as ongoing debates within democratic theory scholarship,
- Draw comparisons between American and French political thought on questions of political ethics,
- Be familiar with key legal and philosophical debates on integrity, accountability, and corruption in democratic institutions,
- Connect the history of political and intellectual thought in France and the United States, with current debates in political ethics and institutional reform,
- Critically analyze normative arguments concerning democracy and its contemporary challenges,
- Develop strong research, analytical and argumentative skills in both oral and written forms.
study_outside:
Students are required to read the two texts posted on Waseda Moodle before each session (about 1–2 hours of preparation), and actively participate in discussions, regardless of whether they are presenting that day. Students should revise the previous class content for 30 minutes before each class.
The final paper and quiz are each expected to take each approximately 1–2 hours of preparation.

Classes will be held in person during the first and last periods and two times online (real-time streaming) in November and December (in total, 11 in person, 2 online, and 1 replaced by an assignment. How can people from different cultural and religious backgrounds have a dialogue for a better mutual understanding? We can no longer ignore the religious aspects to understand present-day global conflicts and deepen dialogues for new cultural developments. Is Christianity capable of exchanging dialogues with different religions and cultures, either monotheistic or polytheistic, such as Japanese culture and religions?
In this seminar, we will mainly deal with the relationship between Christianity and cultural issues such as Literature, Arts, and Thoughts, but also some universal human problems such as Nature and Environment, Discrimination, Search for meaning, Love, and Happiness. A particular interest will be paid to the interactions and dialogues between Christianity and Japanese Religions.
As the subject of their dissertation, the students can choose either a topic concerning mutual understanding between different religious cultures or an author in confrontation with another religious background, as well as any existential human problems or holistic approach to Education.
In the first semester, we will begin by reflecting on religious cultures and environmental problems from the conceptions of nature in the East and the West before dealing with different aspects of Christian Culture and Thoughts in the second semester.
Students will be required to make presentations, participate actively in discussions, and write essays and final papers. We will use primarily Japanese in class.
The class may take more than one koma to ensure enough time for presentations and active discussions.
There may be some extracurricular activities upon the decision of the participants.
